rd-history-partition-independence.title: Partition and Independence, 1947
rd-history-partition-independence.subtitle: The midnight of freedom, a line on a map, and the largest migration in human history

sections.md:
Just before midnight on **14 August 1947**, in the Central Hall of the Constituent Assembly in New Delhi, **Jawaharlal Nehru** rose to speak. His speech, remembered as **'Tryst with Destiny'**, told members that at the stroke of midnight India would awake to life and freedom. Outside, crowds cheered. The next morning the national flag was raised, and on 16 August Nehru hoisted it at the Red Fort.

But in the same days, in Punjab and Bengal, millions of people were leaving homes their families had lived in for generations. Trains crossed the new border carrying refugees; some arrived with passengers who had been killed on the way. **Independence and Partition came together.** A day earlier, on 14 August, **Pakistan** had come into being, with **Muhammad Ali Jinnah** as its Governor-General.

How did freedom, so long fought for, arrive with such suffering? Historians have argued about this for decades. This read sets out the main events and explanations, factually and without taking sides.

> Partition is still within living memory. Many Indian families — Punjabi, Sindhi, Bengali and others — carry its stories. Oral history projects have recorded thousands of them.

check.q: Which speech did Nehru deliver at midnight on 14–15 August 1947?
check.why: Nehru's 'Tryst with Destiny' speech was delivered in the Constituent Assembly as India became independent at midnight.

sections.md:
Historians generally agree that no single event or person 'caused' Partition. Several strands came together over decades:

1. **Separate electorates (1909)**, continued in 1919 and 1935, made politics run along religious lines.
2. **Communal organisations** grew in the 1920s: the Muslim League revived; the **Hindu Mahasabha** (1915) and the **RSS** (1925) were formed; riots occurred in many towns in the 1920s around issues like music before mosques, cow protection, and conversion/reconversion campaigns.
3. **Breakdowns in negotiation:** the Nehru Report (1928) and Jinnah's Fourteen Points (1929) could not be reconciled.
4. **1937 elections and after:** the League did poorly, and after Congress declined to form coalition governments with it in UP, the League argued that Muslims would be dominated in a Congress-led India. Historians debate how important this episode was.
5. **The idea of Pakistan:** the poet **Muhammad Iqbal** in 1930 spoke of a Muslim state in north-west India within a federation; **Choudhry Rahmat Ali**, a student at Cambridge, coined the name 'Pakstan/Pakistan' in 1933. The **Lahore Resolution (23 March 1940)** demanded 'independent states' in Muslim-majority areas.
6. **World War II:** with Congress leaders in jail after 1942, the League extended its organisation; Britain relied on its cooperation.

Historians also debate whether Jinnah truly wanted a fully separate state or used the demand as a bargaining tool for strong safeguards within a united India.

sections.h: The war years: Cripps, Quit India and the INA
sections.md:
When **World War II** began in September 1939, the Viceroy **Lord Linlithgow** declared India at war without consulting Indian leaders. Congress ministries in eight provinces resigned in protest; the Muslim League celebrated a 'Day of Deliverance'.

In **March 1942**, with Japanese armies advancing through Burma, Britain sent **Sir Stafford Cripps**. The **Cripps Mission** offered dominion status *after* the war and allowed provinces to stay out of a future union — an option that seemed to open the door to partition. Congress rejected it; Gandhi is often reported to have called it a 'post-dated cheque'.

On **8 August 1942** the Congress, meeting in Bombay, passed the **Quit India** resolution; Gandhi's call was **'Do or Die'**. The next morning the leaders were arrested. Leaderless, the movement became a vast popular uprising: strikes, attacks on railways and telegraph lines, and **parallel governments** in places such as **Satara** (Maharashtra), **Tamluk** (Bengal) and **Ballia** (UP). Young people such as **Aruna Asaf Ali**, who hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank, and **Jayaprakash Narayan** carried it on underground. The British crushed it within months, with thousands killed and over 90,000 arrested.

Meanwhile **Subhas Chandra Bose**, who had escaped from India in 1941, led the **Indian National Army (INA)** from South-East Asia with Japanese support, under the slogan *Dilli Chalo*. It fought on the Burma–Imphal front in 1944 but was defeated. When INA officers were tried at the **Red Fort in 1945–46**, the whole country rallied for them. In **February 1946**, sailors of the **Royal Indian Navy** mutinied in Bombay. Britain realised it could no longer rely on Indian soldiers to hold India.
keyTerms: Quit India — 1942 mass movement demanding immediate British withdrawal
INA — Indian National Army led by Subhas Chandra Bose
Parallel government — local rule set up by rebels

check.q: What was Gandhi's call in the Quit India movement?
check.why: At the Bombay session on 8 August 1942 Gandhi asked Indians to 'Do or Die' to win freedom.

sections.h: 1946: elections, the Cabinet Mission and Direct Action
sections.md:
In the **1945–46 elections**, Congress swept the general seats and the Muslim League won the great majority of seats reserved for Muslims — strengthening its claim to speak for Muslims.

The British government sent a **Cabinet Mission** (Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps, A. V. Alexander) in March 1946. Its **16 May plan** rejected a separate Pakistan but proposed a **three-tier structure**: a weak Union centre (defence, foreign affairs, communications), provinces grouped into three sections (Section A Hindu-majority; B north-western Muslim-majority; C Bengal and Assam), and the provinces themselves. Both Congress and League first accepted it, but interpreted the grouping differently — the League saw compulsory grouping as the basis of Pakistan; Congress wanted provinces free to opt out. A remark by Nehru in July 1946 that Congress was not bound by every detail alarmed the League, which withdrew its acceptance.

The League called for **'Direct Action Day' on 16 August 1946**. In **Calcutta**, violence broke out and lasted for days; thousands were killed. Violence spread to **Noakhali** in east Bengal (where Gandhi walked village to village for peace), then **Bihar**, **Garhmukteshwar** in UP, and later **Punjab**. The cycle of fear made many people believe living together had become impossible.

An **Interim Government** headed by Nehru took office in September 1946; the League joined in October but the two sides could not work together.

check.q: What did the Cabinet Mission Plan propose?
options: A three-tier federation with grouping of provinces
check.why: The Cabinet Mission proposed a loose union with groups of provinces, avoiding partition, but disagreements over grouping caused it to fail.

check.q: Under the 3 June Plan, which two provinces' assemblies voted on division?
check.why: The 3 June Plan let the Punjab and Bengal assemblies decide whether to partition their provinces, and both chose division.

sections.md:
A British lawyer, **Sir Cyril Radcliffe**, who had never been to India before, was asked to chair two **boundary commissions** — for Punjab and Bengal. Each commission had two Congress and two League nominees, who disagreed; the final decisions were Radcliffe's. He had about **five weeks**, outdated maps and census data, and was told to consider 'contiguous majority areas' and 'other factors'.

The **awards were announced on 17 August 1947 — two days after independence**. So on 15 August, millions of people in border districts did not yet know which country they lived in. Some decisions remain controversial, such as the award of most of **Gurdaspur** district to India and the **Chittagong Hill Tracts** to Pakistan.

Pakistan was created in two wings — **West Pakistan** and **East Pakistan** (East Bengal) — about 1,600 km apart. East Pakistan became independent **Bangladesh** in **1971**.

sections.md:
Partition led to one of the largest migrations in history. Estimates commonly cited are that **10 to 20 million people** were displaced, crossing the new borders in both directions — Hindus and Sikhs moving to India, Muslims to Pakistan. Estimates of deaths range widely, from about **200,000 to 2 million**; historians often say 'up to a million' or more. Exact figures are impossible, because records broke down.

In Punjab, the violence was most intense in August–October 1947. In Bengal, migration continued over many years. Families were separated; property was abandoned; **women** suffered terribly — tens of thousands were abducted on both sides. India and Pakistan later agreed on programmes to recover abducted women, which raised painful questions about choice and belonging.

Refugee camps sprang up — **Kurukshetra** camp housed hundreds of thousands. New towns and colonies grew to resettle refugees: **Faridabad**, **Rajendra Nagar**, **Lajpat Nagar** in Delhi, **Ulhasnagar** near Bombay for Sindhi refugees, and many in West Bengal. Refugees rebuilt lives with remarkable resilience, often starting small businesses from nothing.

In these times many people also **protected neighbours** of other faiths at great risk. Gandhi's fasts in **Calcutta (September 1947)** and **Delhi (January 1948)** helped calm violence.

check.q: Roughly how many people were displaced by Partition, according to common estimates?
check.why: Most estimates suggest that between 10 and 20 million people were displaced across the new borders.

sections.md:
While Delhi celebrated on 15 August 1947, **Gandhi was not there**. He was in **Calcutta**, staying in a run-down house in Beliaghata with **H. S. Suhrawardy**, the former chief minister of Bengal, trying to keep peace between Hindus and Muslims. When violence broke out again on 31 August, he began a fast on 1 September; within days, groups from both communities came to him and laid down weapons. Mountbatten called him a 'one-man boundary force', contrasting him with the large army sent to Punjab.

In **September 1947** Gandhi came to Delhi, which was full of refugees and tense with violence. He visited camps, held prayer meetings where verses from many scriptures were read, and pleaded for Muslims who remained in Delhi to be protected. On **13 January 1948** he began his last fast, asking for communal peace in Delhi and for India to release its share of undivided India's cash balances to Pakistan (₹55 crore), which had been withheld. Leaders signed a peace pledge and he ended the fast on 18 January.

On **30 January 1948**, on his way to the evening prayer meeting at Birla House, Gandhi was shot dead by **Nathuram Godse**, who opposed Gandhi's efforts for Hindu–Muslim unity. Nehru told the nation on radio that 'the light has gone out of our lives'. The shock led the government to ban the RSS for a time (the ban was lifted in 1949), and communal violence in north India subsided for some years.

check.q: Where was Gandhi on 15 August 1947?
check.why: Gandhi spent Independence Day in Calcutta, working and fasting to stop communal violence.

sections.md:
In 1947 there were more than **560 princely states**, covering about two-fifths of the subcontinent. When British paramountcy lapsed, each ruler could in theory choose India, Pakistan or independence.

**Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel**, Home Minister, and his secretary **V. P. Menon** persuaded almost all rulers to sign an **Instrument of Accession**, handing over defence, foreign affairs and communications, before 15 August. Later, states were merged into larger units through further agreements, and rulers were given **privy purses** (abolished in 1971).

Three cases were difficult:
- **Junagadh** (Gujarat): the Nawab acceded to Pakistan though most people were Hindu; after unrest and Indian action, a **plebiscite in February 1948** voted for India.
- **Hyderabad:** the Nizam wanted independence; the Razakars, an armed militia, attacked people; the **Telangana** peasant movement was also active. In **September 1948**, Indian forces moved in ('Operation Polo'), and Hyderabad joined India.
- **Jammu and Kashmir:** Maharaja **Hari Singh** hesitated. In **October 1947** tribal raiders from Pakistan invaded; he signed the Instrument of Accession to India on **26 October 1947**; Indian troops were flown in. The matter went to the UN and fighting ended with a ceasefire on 1 January 1949, leaving part of the state under Pakistani control.

French and Portuguese territories came later: Pondicherry (1954, formally 1962) and Goa (1961).

sections.md:
Independent India faced enormous tasks at once: resettling millions of refugees, dividing assets with Pakistan, integrating states, feeding a poor population and writing a constitution.

**The Constituent Assembly**, elected indirectly by provincial assemblies in 1946, met first on **9 December 1946**. After Partition it had about 299 members. Its **Drafting Committee** was chaired by **Dr B. R. Ambedkar**; **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was the Assembly's president. Debates lasted nearly three years. The Constitution was adopted on **26 November 1949** and came into force on **26 January 1950**, when India became a **republic**. Every adult citizen, man or woman, rich or poor, received the vote — a bold choice in a country where most people could not then read.

**Rehabilitation.** The Ministry of Relief and Rehabilitation gave refugees loans, land left behind by those who had migrated (*evacuee property*), and training. Cities such as **Chandigarh** (designed with Le Corbusier as the new capital of Indian Punjab, since Lahore had gone to Pakistan) and many colonies were built.

**A secular choice.** Despite the violence, India's leaders chose not to become a state of one religion. The Constitution guaranteed equality and freedom of religion to all citizens — Muslims, Hindus, Sikhs, Christians and others alike.

> Did you know? 26 January was chosen because on that date in 1930 the Congress had celebrated 'Purna Swaraj Day', pledging complete independence.
keyTerms: Constituent Assembly — body that wrote India's Constitution
Republic — state whose head is elected, not hereditary
Evacuee property — property left behind by migrants

check.q: When did India's Constitution come into force?
check.why: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950, when India became a republic.

check.q: What source do historians use to recover ordinary people's experiences of Partition?
check.why: Oral history — recorded interviews with survivors — has helped historians understand the experiences of ordinary people, especially women.

parts.md:
Every Diwali, when the house in Delhi's Rajendra Nagar was cleaned top to bottom, Simran's great-grandmother took a small iron key out of a tin box and polished it with a corner of her dupatta. Simran was fifteen before she asked what it opened.

'Our house in Lahore,' Biji said. 'Near Anarkali. A blue door.' She had been nineteen in August 1947. Her family had locked the door, sure they would be back in a few weeks once things calmed down. They took a trunk, some gold sewn into the hems of clothes, and the key.

Biji did not like to describe the journey, and Simran did not press her. She said only that they had walked, then waited for days at a camp, then travelled in a crowded truck; that people were frightened all the time; that she lost track of two cousins who were found, months later, safe in Jalandhar. 'And the Malik family next door,' she added, 'hid my father in their storeroom for one night when a mob came to the lane. They were Muslims. They saved his life. We never saw them again.'

In Delhi they lived for a year in a tent at Kingsway Camp. Her father, once a cloth merchant, sold socks and handkerchiefs from a pushcart. Biji's mother cooked rajma and rice for other refugees for a few annas. Slowly, they saved, and a government loan helped them buy a small plot in a new refugee colony.

'Were you angry?' Simran asked.

Biji thought for a long time. 'For many years I was sad,' she said. 'Then I was busy. We had to build everything again. I learned that people are not one thing. The same summer that some people did terrible things, others risked everything for strangers. Remember both.'

Simran's family is imagined, but stories like Biji's — the key kept for decades, the camp, the pushcart, the neighbour of another faith who sheltered a family — are among the thousands recorded by oral historians and the Partition Museum. Ask the elders in your own family: they may have a story worth writing down.

summary: India became independent at midnight on 14–15 August 1947; Pakistan on 14 August.
Partition had many roots: separate electorates, communal politics, failed negotiations, WWII politics.
The Lahore Resolution (1940) demanded independent Muslim-majority states.
The Cripps Mission (1942) failed; Quit India (August 1942) became a mass uprising; INA trials and the RIN mutiny (1946) shook British confidence.
The Cabinet Mission (1946) proposed a federation with grouping; it collapsed over interpretation.
Direct Action Day (16 Aug 1946) set off riots in Calcutta and beyond.
Attlee set June 1948 as the deadline; Mountbatten's 3 June 1947 plan advanced it to 15 August 1947.
Radcliffe drew the boundaries in about five weeks; awards published 17 August 1947.
10–20 million people were displaced; deaths may have been up to a million or more.
Gandhi worked for peace in Calcutta and Delhi and was assassinated on 30 January 1948.
Patel and V. P. Menon integrated over 560 princely states; Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir were difficult.
The Constitution, drafted under Ambedkar, came into force on 26 January 1950.
Oral history has transformed how Partition is studied.

sections.h: The Satavahanas and trade with Rome
sections.md:
In the Deccan, the **Satavahanas** rose after the Mauryas, ruling from **Pratishthana (Paithan)** on the Godavari. Their most famous king, **Gautamiputra Satakarni** (early 2nd century CE), defeated the Shakas, according to a famous inscription of his mother **Gautami Balashri** at **Nashik**. Satavahana kings were often named after their mothers (Gautamiputra = 'son of Gautami'), an interesting feature, though the kingdom itself followed descent through the father.

They granted land to Brahmins and Buddhist monks; some of the earliest land-grant inscriptions in India are theirs. Buddhist cave monasteries (*chaityas* and *viharas*) at **Karle, Nashik and Bhaja** were cut into the Western Ghats with gifts from merchants and kings.

**Trade with Rome.** Around the 1st century CE, sailors learnt to use the monsoon winds to cross the Arabian Sea directly. A Greek sailors' guide, the **Periplus of the Erythraean Sea**, lists Indian ports: **Barygaza (Bharuch)**, **Sopara**, **Muziris** in Kerala and **Arikamedu** near Puducherry. India exported pepper (called 'black gold'), textiles, gems and ivory. Large hoards of **Roman gold and silver coins** have been found in south India, and Roman amphorae and pottery at Arikamedu.

In western India, the **Shaka** ruler **Rudradaman** (c. 150 CE) recorded in the **Junagadh inscription**, one of the first long inscriptions in Sanskrit, that he repaired the Sudarshana lake, built centuries earlier by the Mauryas.

sections.h: New ways of worship: Mahayana and bhakti
sections.md:
These centuries transformed religion as much as politics.

**Mahayana Buddhism.** Early Buddhism (later called **Theravada** or, by its critics, *Hinayana*, 'lesser vehicle') stressed each person's own effort to reach nibbana. The new **Mahayana** ('great vehicle') tradition made two big changes:

1. The Buddha was now shown as a figure to be worshipped, in statues, not only remembered through symbols.
2. Belief grew in **bodhisattvas** — compassionate beings who had attained enlightenment but chose to stay in the world to help others, such as **Avalokiteshvara** and **Maitreya**.

Mahayana spread along the trade routes into Central Asia, China, Korea and Japan. Chinese pilgrims later travelled to India to collect its texts.

**Bhakti.** At the same time, worship of deities such as **Vishnu**, **Shiva** and the goddess **Durga** grew. Bhakti meant loving devotion to a chosen god, who would respond to the devotee with grace, whatever the devotee's birth or wealth. The **Bhagavad Gita**, part of the Mahabharata, expresses this ideal: Krishna asks Arjuna to give up other paths and take refuge in him. Images of gods were placed in shrines and, later, temples. The **Puranas**, written in simple Sanskrit verse to be read aloud, retold stories of gods and goddesses so that women and shudras, who could not study the Vedas, could hear them.

**Christianity** also reached India: tradition holds that St Thomas came to Kerala in the 1st century CE, and Christian communities grew on the west coast.
keyTerms: Mahayana — 'great vehicle' form of Buddhism with Buddha images and bodhisattvas
Bodhisattva — enlightened being who stays to help others
Bhakti — loving devotion to a personal god
Purana — 'old' text of stories about gods, in simple Sanskrit

check.q: What is a bodhisattva in Mahayana Buddhism?
options: An enlightened being who stays in the world to help others
check.why: Bodhisattvas were believed to have gained enlightenment but chosen to remain in the world out of compassion.

sections.h: Stupas, caves and the merchants who paid for them
sections.md:
Where did people worship, and who paid for these buildings?

**Stupas.** A *stupa* ('mound') is a solid hemispherical dome built over relics — bits of bone, teeth or objects associated with the Buddha or a monk — placed in a small box (the *relic casket*) at its centre. Around it ran a path for **circumambulation** (*pradakshina patha*) enclosed by a railing (*vedika*), with gateways (*toranas*). The great stupa at **Sanchi** (Madhya Pradesh) was enlarged in this period; its four stone gateways, carved in the 1st century BCE–1st century CE, show scenes from the Buddha's life and Jataka stories. **Amaravati** in Andhra Pradesh had a magnificent stupa covered with carved limestone panels; much of it is now in museums in Chennai and London.

Inscriptions on the railings record **who gave money**: ivory carvers of Vidisha paid for one Sanchi gateway; merchants, nuns, monks, farmers and kings gave others. Building and decorating was a community effort and a way for donors to earn merit.

**Rock-cut caves.** In western India, monks lived in **viharas** (cells around a hall) and worshipped in **chaityas** (prayer halls with a small stupa at the end) cut into hills — Karle has one of the largest. Later, at **Ajanta**, the walls were painted with vivid scenes.

**Temples.** By Gupta times, the first **stone temples** appear: small shrines with a **garbhagriha** (the 'womb-house' where the image stood) and a porch, later a tower (**shikhara**) above.
keyTerms: Stupa — dome over relics
Torana — gateway
Pradakshina patha — circular path for walking around the stupa
Garbhagriha — inner shrine of a temple
Shikhara — temple tower

check.q: What is the garbhagriha of a temple?
options: The inner room where the main image is placed
check.why: The garbhagriha, or womb-house, is the inner sanctum holding the image of the deity.

sections.md:
The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim **Faxian** travelled in India from about 399 to 412 CE, during the reign of Chandragupta II, seeking Buddhist texts. He described north Indian towns as prosperous and peaceful, with charitable hospitals and rest houses, light punishments and little interference from officials. He also noted that **'untouchables'** (*chandalas*) had to live outside towns and strike a piece of wood to announce their approach so others could avoid them: a reminder that prosperity was not shared by all.

**Administration.** Gupta kings took grand titles but ruled through many **samantas**, subordinate rulers who paid tribute and supplied troops. Provinces (*bhukti*) were divided into districts (*vishaya*). Local bodies of merchants, bankers and artisans helped run towns. Officials were increasingly paid by **land grants** instead of cash, a trend that would grow in the following centuries.

**Economy.** The Guptas issued the most **gold coins** of any ancient Indian dynasty (called *dinara*, from Roman *denarius*). Land grants to Brahmins and temples expanded farming into new areas.

**Society.** Varna and jati rules were stricter in the law books (*smritis*) of this time. Women of high-status families had fewer rights in texts than earlier, though some, like Prabhavati Gupta, held real power. The first known inscription mentioning a *sati* (at Eran, 510 CE) also dates from this period.

This mix of brilliance and inequality is why historians now hesitate to call the Gupta age simply a 'golden age': it was golden for some.

check.q: Why do historians now hesitate to call the Gupta period simply a 'golden age'?
options: Prosperity and culture coexisted with sharper social inequality
check.why: Evidence like Faxian's description of chandalas shows that the age's achievements were not shared equally.

sections.md:
Whatever we call it, the Gupta age produced work of lasting genius.

**Mathematics and astronomy.** **Aryabhata** wrote the *Aryabhatiya* in **499 CE**, at age 23. He proposed that the Earth rotates on its axis, explained eclipses as shadows rather than demons, and gave π as approximately **3.1416**. The **decimal place-value system** with a symbol for **zero** developed in India during these centuries; the earliest dated inscriptional zero in India is later (Gwalior, 876 CE), and the Bakhshali manuscript also contains a dot for zero, though its dates are debated. **Varahamihira** compiled astronomy and natural knowledge in the *Brihat Samhita* and *Pancha Siddhantika*. India's first satellite (1975) was named *Aryabhata*.

**Medicine.** The *Charaka Samhita* and *Sushruta Samhita* (compiled over earlier centuries) describe diagnosis, herbs and surgery.

**Literature.** **Kalidasa**, perhaps India's greatest Sanskrit poet, wrote the play *Abhijnanashakuntalam*, and the poems *Meghaduta* (a cloud carries a message across India) and *Raghuvamsha*. The **Puranas** took their present shape, and the *Panchatantra* stories spread. **Vishakhadatta** wrote *Mudrarakshasa*. The **Nalanda** monastery-university was founded in the 5th century, traditionally under Kumaragupta I.

**Art and architecture.** Early **stone temples** appear: the **Dashavatara temple at Deogarh** and the temple at Bhitargaon (of brick). The **Ajanta** caves' most famous paintings were made under **Vakataka** patronage in the late 5th century. The **Sarnath Buddha** in the 'preaching' pose is a masterpiece of calm.

And in Delhi stands the **Iron Pillar** (now at the Qutb complex), about 7 m tall, with a Sanskrit inscription of a king called Chandra, usually identified as Chandragupta II. It has resisted rusting for about 1,600 years, thanks to high phosphorus in the iron that forms a protective film.

sections.md:
From the mid-5th century, pressure mounted. The **Hunas** (Hephthalites), from Central Asia, attacked the north-west. **Skandagupta** (c. 455–467 CE) beat them back, and his Junagadh inscription records that he too repaired the Sudarshana lake. But later Huna leaders **Toramana** and **Mihirakula** pushed into north India in the early 6th century, before being defeated by Indian rulers such as **Yashodharman** of Malwa.

Other causes of decline: weak later rulers, powerful **samantas** breaking away, costly wars, and a decline in long-distance trade (some argue the fall of the western Roman empire hurt Indian exports). By the mid-6th century the Gupta empire had dissolved into regional kingdoms: the Maukharis of Kanauj, the later Guptas of Magadha, the Maitrakas of Valabhi, and others.

Yet the Gupta legacy lasted: Sanskrit became the language of courts across India and Southeast Asia, temple Hinduism grew, the decimal system spread, and styles of sculpture shaped art from Afghanistan to Java. In the next reads we follow the south and the early medieval kingdoms that inherited this world.

check.q: Which Central Asian people attacked the Gupta empire in the 5th–6th centuries?
check.why: The Hunas, led later by Toramana and Mihirakula, weakened Gupta control of north India.

parts.md:
Muziris, on the Kerala coast, about 60 CE. Chathan's father owned a small pepper garden in the hills behind the port. Each year, when the south-west monsoon died down and the rain-washed sky turned blue again, the strange ships arrived: tall wooden vessels from the land the Tamil poets called *Yavana* — Greek and Roman sailors from Egypt.

Chathan, twelve, was allowed to help carry sacks to the riverbank warehouses. The black peppercorns, dried on mats in the sun, smelled sharp and warm. 'Those men will pay gold for this,' his father said, 'gold that has crossed half the world.'

The Yavana traders were loud and sunburnt. They brought wine in tall clay jars with pointed bottoms, glassware, coral, and coins stamped with the face of an emperor in a laurel wreath. Chathan's uncle, who weighed goods for the merchants' guild, bit one coin and laughed. 'Pure,' he said. Local goldsmiths sometimes melted such coins into jewellery; others buried them in pots for safety.

One sailor showed Chathan how they had come: straight across the open sea, riding the monsoon wind for forty days, instead of creeping along the coast as their grandfathers had. 'Your wind brings us,' the sailor said in broken Tamil, 'and in winter the other wind takes us home.'

Years later, Chathan, now a merchant himself, travelled east to the port of Arikamedu, where Roman-style pottery was used in the houses and bead-makers drilled tiny glass beads for export. He sent pepper west and cotton cloth east to Southeast Asia. The world, he thought, was a web, and Muziris sat in the middle of it.

Chathan is invented, but Muziris was real: Tamil Sangam poems describe Yavana ships bringing gold and leaving with pepper, a Roman papyrus records a loan for a Muziris cargo, and archaeologists at Pattanam in Kerala — probably part of ancient Muziris — have found amphora fragments and Roman glass. A Roman writer, Pliny, even complained that India drained the empire of gold.

summary: After 185 BCE, Shungas, Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas and Satavahanas ruled different regions.
Menander debated Nagasena in the Milindapanha; Indo-Greek coins carried kings' portraits.
Kanishka of the Kushanas patronised Buddhism and the Fourth Council; the Shaka era (78 CE) is often linked to him.
Gandhara and Mathura schools made early human images of the Buddha.
Satavahanas ruled the Deccan; Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated the Shakas.
Monsoon sailing linked India to Rome; the Periplus names Barygaza and Muziris.
Mahayana Buddhism introduced Buddha images and bodhisattvas; bhakti, the Bhagavad Gita and the Puranas shaped new Hindu worship.
Stupas at Sanchi and Amaravati and caves at Karle were paid for by many donors; the first stone temples appeared.
The Gupta era began 319–320 CE under Chandragupta I.
Harishena's Allahabad prashasti describes Samudragupta's campaigns.
Chandragupta II defeated the Shakas; Faxian visited his empire.
Aryabhata (499 CE) gave π ≈ 3.1416 and said the Earth rotates; Kalidasa wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam and Meghaduta.

rd-history-regional-powers.title: Marathas, Sikhs and the Regional Powers
rd-history-regional-powers.subtitle: As Delhi weakened in the 18th century, new kingdoms rose — from Pune to Lahore, Hyderabad to Mysore

sections.md:
In 1700, a traveller on the road from Delhi to Pune would have passed through one empire. By 1760 the same road crossed lands controlled by Mughal governors who no longer obeyed Delhi, Rajput kings, Jat chiefs and above all the Marathas, whose horsemen collected taxes from Gujarat to Bengal.

The eighteenth century used to be called a 'dark age' between the Mughals and the British. Historians now see it differently: it was a time of **regional states**, many of them prosperous, with thriving trade, banking, art and new forms of government. Broadly, these states fell into three groups:

1. **Successor states** carved out by Mughal governors — **Hyderabad, Awadh, Bengal**.
2. **Watan jagir states** of the Rajputs, who had served the Mughals and now acted more independently.
3. **States born from resistance** to Mughal rule — **Marathas, Sikhs, Jats**.

And there was **Mysore** in the south, which became a powerful military state under Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan.

sections.h: The crisis at the centre after 1707
sections.md:
Why did Delhi lose its grip so quickly after Aurangzeb died in 1707?

**Succession wars.** Aurangzeb's son **Bahadur Shah I** won the throne after fighting his brothers, but died in 1712. In the next seven years, four emperors came and went. Powerful nobles now made and unmade emperors. The **Sayyid brothers**, Abdullah Khan and Husain Ali Khan, were so powerful between 1713 and 1720 that they were called 'king-makers'; they placed **Farrukhsiyar** on the throne and later had him blinded and killed.

**Factions among the nobles.** The Mughal nobility was divided into groups — **Iranis** and **Turanis** (nobles of Iranian and Central Asian origin), Afghans, Indian Muslims and Rajputs — who competed for the best posts and jagirs.

**The jagir crisis.** There was not enough good land to give as jagirs to all the mansabdars. Nobles tried to get rich quickly from the jagirs they did have, often through **ijaradari** (revenue farming), pressing peasants hard. Peasant and zamindar revolts broke out in many areas.

**Invasions.** In **1739** **Nadir Shah** of Iran defeated the Mughal army at **Karnal**, entered Delhi, and plundered it for days; he took away vast treasure including the **Peacock Throne** and the **Kohinoor** diamond. From 1748 to 1767, **Ahmad Shah Abdali** invaded north India repeatedly.

By the mid-18th century, the Mughal emperor still had prestige — rulers everywhere sought his titles and struck coins in his name — but little real power. Under **Shah Alam II** (1759–1806), people joked that his rule ran 'from Delhi to Palam', a village just outside the city.
keyTerms: Sayyid brothers — 'king-makers' of the early 18th century
Irani and Turani — factions of nobles of Iranian and Central Asian origin
Ijaradari — revenue farming

check.q: Who invaded Delhi in 1739 and carried off the Peacock Throne?
check.why: Nadir Shah of Iran defeated the Mughals at Karnal and plundered Delhi in 1739.

sections.h: Shivaji and the making of the Maratha state
sections.md:
**Shivaji** was born in **1630** at **Shivneri** fort near Pune. His father, Shahji Bhonsle, served the Bijapur Sultanate; his mother, **Jijabai**, raised him in the Pune jagir with the help of the administrator Dadoji Kondadev.

From his teens Shivaji began capturing hill forts in the **Sahyadri** (Western Ghats). He relied on the **Mavlas**, hardy peasants of the hills, and on a mobile style of warfare — fast raids, surprise attacks, retreat to forts — often called **ganimi kava** (guerrilla tactics).

Key episodes:
- **1659:** He killed **Afzal Khan**, the Bijapur general, at a meeting below Pratapgad.
- **1663:** A night raid on the Mughal governor **Shaista Khan** in Pune.
- **1664:** Sack of the rich Mughal port of **Surat**.
- **1665:** **Treaty of Purandar** with the Mughal general **Raja Jai Singh**, ceding 23 forts.
- **1666:** Shivaji visited Aurangzeb at **Agra**, was placed under watch, and escaped — tradition says hidden in baskets of sweets.
- **1674:** Crowned **Chhatrapati** at **Raigad**.

Shivaji built a navy on the Konkan coast and forts like **Sindhudurg**. His government had a council of eight ministers, the **Ashtapradhan**, headed by the **Peshwa**. Revenue included **chauth** (one-fourth of the revenue of neighbouring areas, in return for not raiding them) and **sardeshmukhi** (an extra one-tenth claimed as hereditary 'head deshmukh'). He died in 1680.

sections.md:
After Shivaji, his son **Sambhaji** was captured and executed by Aurangzeb in 1689. Sambhaji's brother **Rajaram** and then Rajaram's widow **Tarabai** led resistance. In 1707 Sambhaji's son **Shahu** was released by the Mughals, and he became king at **Satara**.

Under Shahu real power passed to the **Peshwa** (chief minister), whose office became hereditary in the Bhat family:

- **Balaji Vishwanath** (1713–1720) secured from the Mughals the right to collect chauth and sardeshmukhi in the Deccan (1719).
- **Baji Rao I** (1720–1740), a brilliant cavalry general, pushed into Malwa, Gujarat and Bundelkhand and raided up to Delhi in 1737. He defeated the Nizam at Palkhed (1728) and Bhopal (1738).
- **Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb)** (1740–1761) presided over the widest Maratha reach — from Attock in the north-west to Cuttack in the east.

The Maratha state became a **confederacy**: great chiefs ruled their own areas — the **Scindias (Shindes)** at Gwalior, **Holkars** at Indore, **Gaekwads** at Baroda, **Bhonsles** at Nagpur — all nominally under the Peshwa at Pune.

In conquered areas the Marathas often kept local systems but collected chauth and sardeshmukhi. Agriculture and trade grew in Malwa; towns like **Ujjain** and **Indore** became busy commercial centres with Maratha patronage, and **Pune** grew from a small town into a large city.

> Did you know? The Holkar queen **Ahilyabai** (ruled 1767–1795) of Indore is remembered for good administration and for rebuilding temples and ghats across India, including the Kashi Vishwanath temple.

check.q: Which family ruled Indore as part of the Maratha confederacy?
check.why: The Holkars ruled Indore; the Scindias held Gwalior, the Gaekwads Baroda and the Bhonsles Nagpur.

sections.md:
In the 1750s the Marathas moved into Punjab, clashing with **Ahmad Shah Abdali** (Durrani), ruler of Afghanistan, who claimed it. On **14 January 1761**, at the **Third Battle of Panipat**, a Maratha army under **Sadashivrao Bhau** faced Abdali, who had allied with the Rohilla chief Najib-ud-daula and Shuja-ud-daula of Awadh.

The Marathas had been cut off from supplies for weeks and were short of food. Their artillery under Ibrahim Khan Gardi was strong, but the battle turned in the afternoon; the Peshwa's son **Vishwasrao** and Sadashivrao Bhau were killed. The losses were enormous, and the Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao died months later.

Why does it matter? Abdali did not stay to rule; he went home. But the Marathas' northern ambitions were checked for a decade, just when the **English East India Company** was gaining power in Bengal after **Plassey (1757)**. The Marathas recovered under **Madhavrao I** and the minister **Nana Phadnavis**, and **Mahadji Scindia** even controlled the Mughal emperor in Delhi in the 1770s–80s. But internal rivalries and three **Anglo-Maratha Wars** (1775–82, 1803–05, 1817–18) ended Maratha independence; the Peshwa office was abolished in 1818.

sections.h: The Sikhs: from panth to kingdom
sections.md:
The Sikh community grew under the ten Gurus. In **1699**, at **Anandpur**, **Guru Gobind Singh** founded the **Khalsa**, an order of initiated Sikhs who kept the five symbols (the *five Ks*: kesh, kangha, kara, kachera, kirpan). After his death in 1708, **Banda Singh Bahadur** led a peasant uprising in Punjab, struck coins in the name of the Gurus, and abolished the zamindari of Mughal officials in areas he controlled. He was captured and executed in Delhi in 1716.

Through the 18th century, Sikh fighters organised into bands called **misls**, which met twice a year at Amritsar in a **Sarbat Khalsa** to take collective decisions (*gurmata*). They resisted Mughal governors and Abdali's invasions. The misls offered protection to cultivators in return for a tax called **rakhi** — about one-fifth of the produce.

In the late 1790s **Ranjit Singh**, chief of the Sukerchakia misl, united the misls and captured **Lahore in 1799**. He proclaimed himself **Maharaja** in 1801. His kingdom stretched from the Sutlej to the Khyber and included Kashmir and Multan. He modernised his army — the **Fauj-i-Khas** — with European officers, and his court included Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs in high posts. He also gilded the **Harmandir Sahib** at Amritsar, now called the Golden Temple.

After his death in 1839 the kingdom weakened; the British annexed Punjab in **1849** after two **Anglo-Sikh Wars**.
keyTerms: Khalsa — order of initiated Sikhs founded in 1699
Misl — Sikh military band of the 18th century
Rakhi — protection tax (one-fifth of produce)
Sarbat Khalsa — assembly of the whole Sikh community

check.q: Which city did Ranjit Singh capture in 1799?
check.why: Ranjit Singh captured Lahore in 1799, making it the capital of the Sikh kingdom he went on to build.

sections.md:
**Hyderabad.** **Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah**, a top Mughal noble and once wazir in Delhi, became governor of the Deccan and from **1724** ran it as his own state. He brought in skilled soldiers and administrators from the north, but the Nizams fought the Marathas continually.

**Awadh.** **Burhan-ul-Mulk Saadat Khan**, appointed governor in **1722**, combined the offices of subadar, diwan and faujdar, reduced the power of the Mughal-appointed jagirdars, and depended on local bankers. Later Nawabs made **Lucknow** a great centre of culture — architecture, poetry, cuisine and music.

**Bengal.** **Murshid Quli Khan** became effectively independent and moved the capital to **Murshidabad**. He reorganised revenue through **ijaradari**, contracts with revenue farmers, and strict collection. His successors **Alivardi Khan** and **Siraj-ud-daula** ruled a very rich province — rich enough to attract the English East India Company, which defeated Siraj at **Plassey (1757)**.

These governors kept sending formal respect and sometimes tribute to Delhi and used Mughal titles, but made appointments, fought wars and raised taxes as they pleased. A common feature of all three was a close relationship with **bankers and merchants**, who lent money to the state and were trusted to collect revenue.

check.q: Who founded the independent state of Awadh in 1722?
check.why: Burhan-ul-Mulk Saadat Khan was appointed governor of Awadh in 1722 and turned it into a practically independent state.

sections.md:
**Rajputs.** Many Rajput kings had been high mansabdars. In the 18th century rulers like **Sawai Raja Jai Singh** of Amber built strong states. Jai Singh founded the city of **Jaipur** in 1727 and built astronomical observatories, the **Jantar Mantar**, at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi.

**Jats.** Peasants and landholders around Delhi, Agra and Mathura, the Jats became a political power under **Churaman** and especially **Suraj Mal** (d. 1763), who built forts and a palace complex at **Bharatpur** and **Deeg**.

**Mysore.** **Haidar Ali**, a soldier, took control of the Wodeyar kingdom around 1761. His son **Tipu Sultan** (ruled 1782–1799) modernised his army with rockets, built a navy, introduced new coins and calendar, and planted mulberry for silk. He sought help from the French against the British. Mysore fought four **Anglo-Mysore Wars**; Tipu died defending **Srirangapatna** in **1799**.

> Did you know? Rockets used by Mysore's army impressed the British so much that some were taken to Britain and studied; they influenced the British Congreve rocket.

check.q: Which ruler built the Jantar Mantar observatories?
check.why: Sawai Raja Jai Singh of Amber, founder of Jaipur, built the Jantar Mantar observatories in several cities.

sections.h: Money, art and everyday life in the regional states
sections.md:
The eighteenth century was not only about battles. In many regions, life went on and even flourished.

**Bankers.** The great banking house of the **Jagat Seths** of Murshidabad ('bankers of the world') managed the Bengal treasury, minted coins and lent huge sums to nawabs — and later to the East India Company. Bankers' bills of exchange called **hundis** moved money across India safely without carrying coins: a merchant in Surat could pay a hundi that would be honoured in Varanasi or Dhaka.

**Trade and crafts.** Textile production in Bengal, Gujarat and the Coromandel coast remained huge. New market towns (*qasbas* and *ganjs*) grew along roads and rivers.

**Culture.** As artists left a declining Delhi, they found patrons in regional courts. **Lucknow** became famous for Urdu poetry, Kathak dance, thumri music and its cuisine. **Hyderabad** built palaces and gardens. In the Himalayan foothills, small Rajput courts patronised the beautiful **Pahari** painting schools of **Basohli** and **Kangra**, which often showed Radha and Krishna. Rajasthani painting flourished at Kishangarh, Mewar and Bundi. Marathi literature, including the *bakhars* (historical chronicles) and the ballads called *powadas*, celebrated Maratha heroes.

**Religion.** In Punjab the Sikh panth grew; in Maharashtra the **Varkari** tradition of pilgrimage to **Pandharpur** remained strong; Sufi shrines attracted people of all faiths across the north.

So while the Mughal centre weakened, many regions prospered — which is why historians speak of **'decentralisation'** rather than simply 'decline'.
keyTerms: Hundi — bill of exchange used to transfer money
Jagat Seth — title of Bengal's leading banking family
Pahari painting — miniature painting of the Himalayan hill states

check.q: What was a hundi?
options: A bill of exchange for transferring money
check.why: Hundis were written notes that let merchants transfer money across long distances without carrying coins.

sections.h: Why did the regional powers fall to the British?
sections.md:
By the mid-19th century almost all these states had been conquered or made subordinate by the English East India Company. Reasons historians suggest include:

- **Rivalries** among Indian states — Marathas, Nizam and Mysore often fought each other and sometimes allied with the Company.
- **Finance:** the Company had the revenue of Bengal and access to credit from Indian bankers.
- **Disciplined infantry and artillery**, paid regularly, on the European model — which Indian states also copied, sometimes successfully.
- **Subsidiary alliances** introduced by **Lord Wellesley** (1798): a ruler kept Company troops and paid for them, gave up foreign policy and accepted a British Resident. Hyderabad was among the first to accept.
- **Internal disputes** over succession that the Company exploited.

Yet the 18th century left a rich legacy: Lucknow's culture, Jaipur's planned city, Maratha administration and records, Sikh institutions, and the idea that India was a land of many political centres.

check.q: Who introduced the system of subsidiary alliance?
check.why: Lord Wellesley introduced subsidiary alliances in 1798, making Indian rulers pay for Company troops and accept a British Resident.

parts.md:
Pune, 1745. Govind, fourteen, had been apprenticed to a sahukar — a moneylender and banker — in the bustling Budhwar Peth market for less than a year when his master handed him a folded paper sealed with red wax. 'This is a hundi,' said Sheth Mahadev. 'It is worth two thousand rupees. Take it to our partner's agent in Ujjain. Do not lose it — and do not let anyone know what it is.'

Govind stared. Two thousand rupees, in one piece of paper? 'Why not send the coins?' he asked.

'Because coins are heavy, and roads have thieves,' the Sheth laughed. 'This paper is useless to a thief. Only our agent will pay against it, after checking my seal and my handwriting.'

Govind travelled with a caravan of bullock carts carrying cloth and salt, guarded by a dozen armed men. On the way, they met a troop of Maratha horsemen riding north towards Malwa, where the Peshwa's chiefs were collecting chauth. At a river crossing, the carts paid a toll to an official of the Holkars. In one village, peasants complained that they had paid tax twice that year — once to a Mughal officer and once to a Maratha one. Govind listened, and began to understand that the map of power was changing under his feet.

At Ujjain he found the agent's shop near the Mahakal temple. The old man examined the seal with a magnifying glass, compared the handwriting with a letter in his box, and nodded. 'Good,' he said. 'Now I will pay a cloth merchant here, who owes your Sheth's client in Pune. Not a single coin needs to travel the whole road.'

Back in Pune months later, Govind told his master what he had seen. 'Kings fight over land,' the Sheth said, 'but they all need us. The Peshwa borrows from bankers to pay his soldiers. The Nizam borrows. Even the Company men in Bombay borrow. Our paper travels further than any army.'

Govind is imagined, but hundis, caravans, Maratha tolls and sahukars lending to rulers are well documented in 18th-century records. Historians use bankers' account books — some still preserved in family archives — to understand how money and trade kept flowing even as empires rose and fell.

summary: After 1707, regional states emerged as Mughal power weakened.
Succession wars, the Sayyid brothers, noble factions, the jagir crisis and Nadir Shah's invasion (1739) weakened the Mughal centre.
Hyderabad (1724), Awadh (1722) and Bengal were successor states founded by Mughal governors.
Shivaji (1630–1680) built a Maratha kingdom using hill forts and swift cavalry; crowned at Raigad in 1674.
The Ashtapradhan, chauth and sardeshmukhi were key features of Maratha government.
Peshwas Balaji Vishwanath and Baji Rao I expanded Maratha power; it became a confederacy.
The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) checked Maratha power in the north.
Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699; Banda Bahadur led a revolt.
Sikh misls collected rakhi; Ranjit Singh united them and took Lahore in 1799.
Sawai Jai Singh founded Jaipur; Suraj Mal led the Jats at Bharatpur.
Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan made Mysore a strong military state; Tipu died in 1799.
Bankers like the Jagat Seths, hundis, regional courts and painting schools show the century's prosperity.
Rivalries and subsidiary alliances helped the British subdue the regional powers.

rd-history-social-reform.title: Social Reform Movements of the 19th Century
rd-history-social-reform.subtitle: Reformers who argued, wrote, petitioned and built schools to change how Indians lived

sections.md:
In 1811, in Bengal, a young man watched as his brother's widow was burned on her husband's funeral pyre — the practice called **sati**. Tradition says this experience moved **Rammohun Roy** to spend years campaigning against it. Whether or not every detail of the story is exact, his campaign was real, and in **1829** the Governor-General **Lord William Bentinck** made sati illegal in Bengal Presidency.

The nineteenth century in India was an age of argument. New printing presses produced newspapers, pamphlets and books in Bengali, Marathi, Urdu, Tamil, Hindi and English. People debated: What do our scriptures really say? Should widows remarry? Should girls go to school? Is caste justified? Reformers looked both to ancient texts and to new ideas of reason, equality and human rights.

This read meets the reformers — and also notes their limits and critics.

check.q: In which year was sati banned in Bengal Presidency?
check.why: Lord William Bentinck banned sati in 1829, after a long campaign by Raja Rammohun Roy and others.

sections.h: Why reform now? Print, schools and colonial rule
sections.md:
Several new forces came together in the early 1800s.

**The printing press.** Presses at **Serampore** (run by Baptist missionaries from 1800) and in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras made books cheap. For the first time, debates could reach thousands of readers. Rammohun Roy's Bengali weekly *Sambad Kaumudi* (1821) and Persian *Mirat-ul-Akhbar* argued for reform; conservatives replied in *Samachar Chandrika*. Readers argued in letters pages.

**Colonial education debates.** British officials disagreed about what to teach Indians. **Orientalists** such as **William Jones**, who founded the **Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784)**, admired Sanskrit and Persian learning; institutions like the Calcutta Madrasa (1781) and Benaras Sanskrit College (1791) followed. **Anglicists** wanted English and Western science. In **1835**, **Thomas Babington Macaulay's Minute on Education** dismissed Eastern learning, and the English Education Act made English the medium of higher education. **Wood's Despatch (1854)** set out a plan for schools in Indian languages up to university level, and in **1857** universities were founded at **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras**.

**Missionaries** opened schools, including for girls and lower castes, and criticised Indian customs — sometimes in insulting ways that provoked Indians to defend and reform their own traditions.

**A new middle class** of lawyers, teachers, clerks and journalists, educated in English and in Indian languages, wanted their society to be both modern and true to its own heritage.

Reformers did not simply copy the West: most argued from Indian scriptures and traditions, showing that customs like sati or child marriage had no sound basis in them.
keyTerms: Orientalist — scholar who admired and studied Asian learning
Anglicist — supporter of English education
Wood's Despatch — 1854 education plan
Asiatic Society — learned society founded in Calcutta in 1784

check.q: Which 1835 document argued for English education in India?
check.why: Macaulay's Minute of 1835 argued that English should be the medium of higher education, and the Act of that year followed it.

sections.h: Rammohun Roy and the Brahmo Samaj
sections.md:
**Raja Rammohun Roy** (1772–1833) knew Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and English. He argued that the **Upanishads** taught worship of one formless God, and that later practices like idol worship and sati were not essential to Hinduism. He translated scriptures into Bengali to let people read them for themselves.

In **1828** he founded the **Brahmo Sabha**, later called the **Brahmo Samaj**, for monotheistic worship without images. He supported English and science education, helped found institutions in Calcutta, and campaigned for women's property rights and press freedom. He died in Bristol, England, in 1833.

After him, **Debendranath Tagore** (father of Rabindranath) strengthened the Samaj, and **Keshab Chandra Sen** spread it across India. Keshab's campaign led to the **Native Marriage Act of 1872** (sometimes called the Brahmo Marriage Act), which allowed inter-caste marriages and set minimum ages. The Samaj later split, partly because Keshab married his young daughter to a prince, against the Samaj's own rules.

In the same years, the **Young Bengal** movement of students at Hindu College, inspired by their teacher **Henry Louis Vivian Derozio** (1809–1831), questioned all tradition and authority with youthful passion.
keyTerms: Monotheism — belief in one God
Brahmo Samaj — reform society founded by Rammohun Roy (1828)

check.q: Which scriptures did Rammohun Roy use to argue for worship of one God?
check.why: Rammohun Roy drew on the Upanishads to argue that original Hindu philosophy taught worship of one formless God.

sections.h: The other side: opponents and debates
sections.md:
Reform was never one-sided. Every campaign met determined opposition, and understanding the opponents helps us understand the reformers.

**The Dharma Sabha.** When sati was banned in 1829, orthodox leaders in Calcutta, including **Radhakanta Deb**, formed the **Dharma Sabha** (1830) and petitioned the Privy Council in London to overturn the ban. They argued that the government had promised not to interfere in religion. The appeal failed in 1832; Rammohun Roy, then in England, argued the other side.

**Widow remarriage.** When Vidyasagar petitioned for widow remarriage, a counter-petition opposing it collected even more signatures than his. After the 1856 Act, the first widow remarriages were attended by crowds, some supporters, some jeering. Families of reformers were sometimes boycotted by their caste.

**Arguments used by each side.**

| Reformers argued | Opponents argued |
|---|---|
| Ancient texts do not require the custom | Long-standing custom is itself sacred |
| Reason and compassion demand change | Foreigners should not change Indian religion |
| Women suffer needlessly | Reform will break up families and caste order |

**Reform and nationalism.** By the 1880s, some nationalists, like **Tilak**, felt that social reform should come from within society, not through laws passed by a foreign government, and that political freedom must come first. Others, like **Ranade** and **Gokhale**, argued that a nation could not be free while it kept women and lower castes in bondage. This debate between 'social reform first' and 'political reform first' ran through the national movement.

> Notice: even conservatives used the new tools of print, petitions and associations — the age of reform changed how *everyone* did politics.
keyTerms: Dharma Sabha — orthodox society formed in 1830 to oppose the sati ban
Petition — formal written request signed by many people

check.q: What was the Dharma Sabha?
options: A reform society founded by Phule
An orthodox body opposing the ban on sati
check.why: The Dharma Sabha was formed in Calcutta in 1830 by orthodox Hindus to challenge the 1829 sati ban.

sections.md:
**Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** (1820–1891) was a Sanskrit scholar and principal of Sanskrit College, Calcutta. Using ancient texts, he argued that widows could remarry. He collected thousands of signatures, and the **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act** was passed in **1856**. He personally arranged and paid for many such marriages — including his own son's to a widow — at great personal cost.

Vidyasagar also opened many schools for girls in Bengal and wrote **Barnaparichay**, a Bengali primer still remembered today. He campaigned against child marriage and polygamy.

In western India, **Vishnushastri Pandit** founded a widow remarriage association in the 1860s, and later **D. K. Karve** (who married a widow himself) started a widows' home and eventually a women's university in Pune (SNDT, 1916). In the south, **Kandukuri Veeresalingam** promoted widow remarriage in the Telugu-speaking areas.

check.q: Which law was passed in 1856 after Vidyasagar's campaign?
check.why: The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856 legalised the remarriage of Hindu widows after Vidyasagar's petition campaign.

sections.h: Girls at school and women's own voices
sections.md:
Many families in the 19th century feared that schooling would make girls 'disobedient' or that, outside the home, they would be exposed to bad influences. Even so, change came.

**Schools.** The **Bethune School** for girls opened in Calcutta in **1849**, supported by Vidyasagar. In Pune, the Phules' school had opened a year earlier. In the north, the **Arya Samaj** opened girls' schools in Punjab, and in Bhopal the **Begums** (women rulers of the state) promoted girls' education and founded a primary school for girls at Aligarh. Many women were also taught at home by liberal fathers or husbands.

**Firsts.** **Kadambini Ganguly** and **Chandramukhi Basu** became among the first women graduates in India (Calcutta University, 1883). **Anandibai Joshi** studied medicine in the USA and became one of the first Indian women doctors (1886); Kadambini Ganguly also practised medicine.

**Women writers.** Women began to write about their own lives. **Rashsundari Debi**, a housewife in rural Bengal, secretly taught herself to read by candlelight in the kitchen, hiding a page of a sacred book; she later wrote **Amar Jiban** (1876), the first full autobiography in Bengali. Pandita Ramabai, Tarabai Shinde and later Begum Rokeya used their pens to question how society treated women.

In the early 20th century, women formed their own associations: the **Bharat Stree Mahamandal** (1910, Sarala Devi Chaudhurani) and later the **All India Women's Conference** (1927).
keyTerms: Amar Jiban — Rashsundari Debi's autobiography (1876)
Bethune School — early girls' school in Calcutta (1849)

check.q: Who wrote Amar Jiban, the first full autobiography in Bengali?
check.why: Rashsundari Debi taught herself to read in secret and later wrote Amar Jiban, published in 1876.

sections.h: Western India: Prarthana Samaj, Phule and Ranade
sections.md:
In **Bombay**, the **Prarthana Samaj** (1867), associated with **M. G. Ranade** and **R. G. Bhandarkar**, promoted monotheistic worship, inter-caste dining and marriage, widow remarriage and women's education, drawing on the Marathi bhakti tradition. In Bombay, the **Paramhans Mandali** (1840) had earlier worked secretly against caste.

The most radical voice came from **Jyotirao Phule** (1827–1890) of Pune, from the Mali (gardener) community. He argued that the caste system was an injustice imposed by upper castes, and that so-called low castes and untouchables were the real heirs of India. With his wife **Savitribai Phule**, he opened a school for girls in **1848** in Pune — Savitribai became one of India's first women teachers, facing abuse in the streets on her way to school. In **1873** Phule founded the **Satyashodhak Samaj** (Society of Truth Seekers) for caste equality, and wrote **Gulamgiri** ('Slavery', 1873), comparing caste oppression to slavery in America.

**Pandita Ramabai** (1858–1922), a Sanskrit scholar, wrote about the condition of upper-caste Hindu women and founded the **Sharada Sadan** for widows. **Tarabai Shinde** wrote *Stri Purush Tulana* (1882), a sharp critique of how society judged women and men differently.

check.why: Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873 to fight caste discrimination and promote equality.

sections.h: Dayananda and the Arya Samaj; Vivekananda
sections.md:
**Swami Dayananda Saraswati** (1824–1883) from Gujarat founded the **Arya Samaj** in Bombay in **1875**; it became strongest in Punjab. His slogan was 'Back to the Vedas'. He held that the Vedas were the true source of knowledge, and opposed idol worship, rituals, child marriage and caste by birth. His book **Satyarth Prakash** set out his ideas. The Samaj supported widow remarriage and women's education and opened **Dayanand Anglo-Vedic (DAV)** schools and colleges (the first in Lahore, 1886). Its *shuddhi* movement to bring converts back to Hinduism later became controversial in a context of growing religious competition.

**Swami Vivekananda** (1863–1902), disciple of the mystic **Ramakrishna Paramahamsa**, spoke at the **World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893**, where his address presented Vedanta to a Western audience. In **1897** he founded the **Ramakrishna Mission**, combining spirituality with social service — schools, hospitals, famine relief. He argued that serving the poor was serving God.

The **Theosophical Society**, founded in New York in 1875 and moved to **Adyar (Madras)** in 1882, praised ancient Indian thought; **Annie Besant** became a leading figure in India and later in the national movement.

check.q: Where did Vivekananda deliver his famous address in 1893?
check.why: Vivekananda addressed the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893.

sections.h: Reform among Muslims, Sikhs and Parsis
sections.md:
**Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** (1817–1898) believed Muslims needed modern Western education. He founded the **Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College** at **Aligarh** in **1875**, which became **Aligarh Muslim University** in 1920. The **Aligarh movement** promoted science, rational interpretation of religion and Urdu journalism.

Other Muslim currents included the **Deoband** seminary (1866), which focused on traditional religious learning and opposed Western influence, and the **Ahmadiyya** movement. Reformers like **Mumtaz Ali** argued for women's rights in Islam, and **Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain** started a girls' school in Calcutta (1911) and wrote *Sultana's Dream* (1905), a science-fiction story imagining women ruling a peaceful land.

Among **Sikhs**, the **Singh Sabha** movement (Amritsar 1873, Lahore 1879) promoted education and a distinct Sikh identity; later the **Akali** movement (1920s) won control of gurdwaras from hereditary priests (mahants).

Among **Parsis**, the **Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha** (1851), with **Dadabhai Naoroji** among its founders, promoted women's education and reform of customs.

sections.h: The south and the fight against caste
sections.md:
In Kerala, **Sree Narayana Guru** (1856–1928), from the Ezhava community, preached 'one caste, one religion, one God for humanity'. In 1888 he consecrated a Shiva idol at **Aruvippuram** — a defiant act, since priestly rules barred him. The **SNDP Yogam** (1903) spread his ideas of education and self-respect.

In Tamil Nadu, **E. V. Ramaswamy Naicker ('Periyar')** launched the **Self-Respect Movement** in **1925**, challenging caste, Brahmanical dominance and women's subordination. The **Vaikom Satyagraha (1924–25)** in Travancore demanded that lower castes be allowed to use roads near a temple; leaders included **T. K. Madhavan** and **K. Kelappan**, and Periyar and Gandhi both took part.

**B. R. Ambedkar** (1891–1956), born into the Mahar community, became one of India's most educated people and fought untouchability through law and protest — the **Mahad Satyagraha (1927)** to drink from a public tank, and the **Kalaram temple entry movement (1930)** at Nashik. He would later chair the Drafting Committee of the Constitution.

check.q: Who said 'one caste, one religion, one God for humanity'?
check.why: Sree Narayana Guru of Kerala preached this message of human unity and fought caste discrimination.

check.why: The Child Marriage Restraint (Sarda) Act of 1929 fixed minimum marriage ages at 14 for girls and 18 for boys.

parts.md:
East Bengal, around 1830. The kitchen was the only place Rashsundari could be alone. She had been married at twelve and sent to her husband's village, where she cooked from before dawn until late at night for a large household. Women of respectable families, people said, should not read; reading would bring bad luck.

But Rashsundari longed to read the sacred book her husband kept, the *Chaitanya Bhagavat*. One day, when the book had been left out, she quietly took a single page and hid it in the kitchen, under the edge of a cooking pot.

She remembered a few letters from listening to boys chanting their lessons when she was a child. Now, between tasks, she would glance at the page and match the shapes in her memory. When her son practised writing on a palm leaf, she watched and memorised more letters. Slowly, letter by letter, then word by word, she began to read — always in secret, always in the smoky kitchen, so that no one would scold her.

It took years. But one day she could read the whole page, and then the whole book.

Decades later, as an old woman, Rashsundari Debi wrote the story of her life. *Amar Jiban* ('My Life') was published in 1876 — the first full autobiography written in Bengali. In it she described not only her secret reading but her fears, her household work and her faith.

This story is told in our own words from what historians know of her book. It shows something important about the age of reform: change did not come only from famous men passing laws in Calcutta. It also came from women who, quietly and bravely, claimed the right to learn — sometimes with nothing but a stolen page and a kitchen fire.

summary: Print, colonial education debates, missionaries and a new middle class fuelled reform in the 19th century.
Orientalists and Anglicists disagreed; Macaulay's Minute (1835) favoured English; universities were founded in 1857.
Rammohun Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828) and campaigned against sati, banned in 1829.
Orthodox bodies like the Dharma Sabha opposed reform; the 'social reform first or political reform first' debate divided nationalists.
Vidyasagar's campaign led to the Widow Remarriage Act (1856).
Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a girls' school (1848); Satyashodhak Samaj (1873).
Women's education grew; Rashsundari Debi, Kadambini Ganguly and Anandibai Joshi were pioneers.
Prarthana Samaj (1867) worked in Bombay; Pandita Ramabai and Tarabai Shinde wrote on women's lives.
Dayananda founded the Arya Samaj (1875): 'Back to the Vedas'.
Vivekananda spoke at Chicago (1893) and founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897).
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's Aligarh movement promoted modern education for Muslims; Singh Sabha and Parsi reformers worked within their communities.
Sree Narayana Guru, Periyar and Ambedkar fought caste discrimination.
Reform had limits but laid foundations for equality in the Constitution.

rd-history-south-indian-kingdoms.title: South Indian Kingdoms: Sangam, Pallavas and Cholas
rd-history-south-indian-kingdoms.subtitle: Tamil poets, rock-cut temples, a navy across the Bay of Bengal and village councils that voted

sections.md:
Imagine a poem written about two thousand years ago in Tamil. A woman waits for her lover on a seashore; the screw-pines are flowering; fishermen's boats come home at dusk. Another poem praises a king who gave elephants to bards. A third mourns a hero fallen in a cattle raid, his memory marked by a carved stone.

These are poems of the **Sangam** collections, the earliest Tamil literature. Tradition says they were composed at three great assemblies (*sangams*) of poets held at Madurai under the patronage of the **Pandya** kings. Historians treat the story of the three sangams as legend, but the poems are real and precious. Most scholars date them roughly between **the 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE**.

The collections include the **Ettuthokai** ('Eight Anthologies') and **Pattuppattu** ('Ten Idylls'). The grammar **Tolkappiyam** is linked to the same tradition. Slightly later come two great epics, **Silappadikaram** (story of Kannagi, whose anklet leads to justice) and **Manimekalai** (her daughter's Buddhist path), and the ethical classic **Tirukkural** by **Tiruvalluvar**, with 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love.

Sangam poets divided poems into **akam** ('inner': love) and **puram** ('outer': war, kings, generosity). They also mapped the land into five **tinai** (landscapes), each with its own flower, mood and way of life.

head: Tinai
Landscape
Life
Mood (akam)
fig.caption: The five tinai of Sangam poetry: a geography of feelings.

check.q: In Sangam poetry, 'puram' poems are mainly about:
check.why: Puram ('outer') poems deal with public matters like war, rulers and generosity, while akam poems are about love.

sections.md:
Sangam poems speak of three ruling lineages, the **muvendar** ('three crowned kings'). Ashoka's edicts in the 3rd century BCE already mention the Cholas, Pandyas and Keralaputras (Cheras) as neighbours beyond his empire.

| Dynasty | Region | Capital / port | Emblem |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cholas** | Kaveri delta | Uraiyur; port Puhar (Kaveripattinam) | Tiger |
| **Pandyas** | Madurai and the far south | Madurai; port Korkai | Fish |
| **Cheras** | Kerala coast | Vanji; port Muziris | Bow |

A celebrated early Chola king, **Karikala**, is credited in tradition with defeating rivals at Venni and building embankments on the Kaveri; the **Kallanai** (Grand Anicut) near Thanjavur is traditionally linked to him and is still in use, though it has been rebuilt many times.

Besides the three kings there were many **velir**, powerful chiefs, famed for their gifts to poets. Chiefs and kings rewarded poets and bards (*panar*, *viraliyar*) with gold, elephants and land; the poets in return kept their names alive. Gifts and plunder from raids, rather than regular taxes, were important sources of royal wealth.

**Hero stones** (*nadukal*) were set up for warriors who died defending cattle or villages, a practice that continued for centuries.

**Trade.** Pepper from the Chera coast, pearls from the Pandya sea at Korkai, fine cotton and gems went to Rome, Southeast Asia and China. Roman coins and pottery at **Arikamedu** and the **Muziris papyrus** (a Greek contract about a shipment from Muziris) prove how far this commerce reached. Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions in caves record gifts to Jain and Buddhist monks.

sections.md:
After the Sangam age, a period sometimes said to be under the **Kalabhras** (about whom little is known) gave way to new powers. From the 6th to the 9th century, the **Pallavas** ruled northern Tamil Nadu from **Kanchipuram**, while the **Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi)** ruled the western Deccan. The two fought for generations.

- **Mahendravarman I** (c. 600–630 CE), a poet-king who wrote the Sanskrit comedy *Mattavilasa Prahasana*, began **rock-cut temples** in Tamil Nadu. Tradition says he turned from Jainism to Shaivism under the influence of the saint Appar.
- The Chalukya king **Pulakeshin II**, whose victories are praised in the **Aihole inscription** (634 CE), also defeated the north Indian emperor Harsha on the Narmada, and attacked Kanchi.
- **Narasimhavarman I Mamalla** (c. 630–668 CE) struck back, capturing **Vatapi** around 642 CE, where Pulakeshin II is believed to have died. The Chinese pilgrim **Xuanzang** visited Kanchi in his reign.

The port town **Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram)** carries his title. Its monuments, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, include:

- the **Pancha Rathas**, five temples each carved from a single rock;
- the huge relief **'Descent of the Ganga'** or **'Arjuna's Penance'**, with elephants, sages and a natural cleft for water;
- the **Shore Temple**, built of stone blocks under **Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha** (c. 700 CE), who also built the **Kailasanatha temple** at Kanchi.

The Pallavas used **Grantha script** for Sanskrit, an ancestor of scripts used in Southeast Asia, where Pallava-style writing appears in early inscriptions.

sections.h: The Deccan neighbours: Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas
sections.md:
South Indian history cannot be understood without the Deccan plateau to the north of the Tamil country.

**The Chalukyas of Badami (c. 543–753 CE)** ruled from **Vatapi (Badami)** in present-day Karnataka. Their temple-building experiments survive in three nearby places: **Aihole**, sometimes called a 'cradle of Indian temple architecture', with more than a hundred temples; **Badami**, with rock-cut cave temples; and **Pattadakal**, a UNESCO site where temples in both the northern (*nagara*) and southern (*dravida*) styles stand side by side. The **Aihole inscription** was composed by the poet **Ravikirti** in praise of Pulakeshin II; it tells how Pulakeshin stopped Harsha's advance in the south.

**The Rashtrakutas (c. 753–973 CE).** In the mid-8th century a Chalukya feudatory, **Dantidurga**, overthrew his overlords and founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty. An inscription says he performed a ritual called *hiranya-garbha* ('golden womb'), in which a person was believed to be 'reborn' as a kshatriya — an example of how men of other backgrounds claimed royal status. The Rashtrakutas later ruled from **Manyakheta**.

Their most astonishing monument is the **Kailasa temple at Ellora**, carved under **Krishna I** in the 8th century. It was cut downwards from the top of a single rock hill — a whole two-storeyed temple, courtyard and elephants, made by removing stone rather than adding it.

**Amoghavarsha I** (c. 814–878 CE) was a patron of Kannada and Jain learning; the Kannada work on poetics *Kavirajamarga* is associated with his court.

The Rashtrakutas, the **Palas** of Bengal and the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** of the north fought for nearly two centuries over the rich city of **Kanauj** — a contest historians call the **tripartite struggle**.
keyTerms: Nagara / dravida — northern / southern temple styles
Hiranya-garbha — ritual of 'rebirth' as a kshatriya
Tripartite struggle — Rashtrakuta–Pala–Pratihara contest for Kanauj

check.why: Under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I, craftsmen cut the entire temple out of one rock hill, working downwards.

sections.h: Saints and songs: the Bhakti movement begins
sections.md:
Something remarkable happened in the Tamil country between the 6th and 9th centuries. Wandering poet-saints sang of passionate, personal love for God in the people's language, Tamil, travelling from temple to temple.

- The **Nayanars**, 63 devotees of **Shiva**, among them **Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar** (their hymns form the *Tevaram*), and later **Manikkavachakar**. One Nayanar, **Karaikkal Ammaiyar**, was a woman.
- The **Alvars**, 12 devotees of **Vishnu**, whose hymns were later collected as the *Nalayira Divya Prabandham*. They included **Andal**, a woman saint whose songs are still sung in the month of Margazhi.

The saints came from many backgrounds, including farmers and communities considered 'low' by caste rules, though in practice caste did not disappear. Their message was that sincere devotion mattered more than ritual or birth.

This **bhakti** movement transformed Hinduism. It gave temples a central role, encouraged music and dance, and inspired later bhakti saints across India, from Kabir to Mirabai. Kings like the Pallavas and Cholas built and endowed temples associated with these saints' songs.

check.q: The Alvars were devotees of:
check.why: The twelve Alvars sang devotional hymns to Vishnu, while the Nayanars were devotees of Shiva.
