check.q: A uniformed 'officer' on a video call says you are under digital arrest and must pay. What is correct?
check.why: There is no such thing as a video-call arrest settled by payment; it is a scam to be reported on 1930.

sections.md:
You can make UPI even safer by building fences:

- **Keep a small 'spending' account.** Many seniors keep pension and FDs in one account, and link UPI to a separate savings account with just a few thousand rupees. If anything goes wrong, the loss is small. Discuss with your bank.
- **Set daily limits.** Many apps and banks let you lower your daily UPI limit — say ₹5,000.
- **App lock.** Turn on fingerprint lock for the UPI app.
- **SMS alerts.** Make sure your bank sends an SMS for every transaction. Read them.
- **UPI Lite** in several apps lets you pay small amounts (a few hundred rupees) from a small pre-loaded wallet without a PIN each time — convenient for tea and vegetables, but keep the balance low.
- **Phone screen lock.** A PIN or fingerprint on the phone itself is your first gate. Don't hand an unlocked phone to strangers who 'need to make one call'.
- **Lost phone?** Call your bank to block UPI and your mobile operator to block the SIM at once. Your money is safe as long as no one knows the UPI PIN, but blocking is quick insurance.

Limits and features are set by NPCI and your bank and do change over time, so check the current rules in your app or at the branch.

> Did you know? UPI also works on simple keypad phones through **UPI 123PAY** and by dialling *99#, so even a basic phone can make payments.

Once you are comfortable, UPI apps can pay many monthly bills from your armchair:

- Electricity, water, piped gas, LPG cylinder booking
- Mobile and DTH recharge
- Broadband, insurance premium, even some municipal taxes

Look for 'Bill payments' or 'Recharge' in the app. The system behind it, **Bharat BillPay (BBPS)**, gives a reference number for every payment — note it down or screenshot it.

**A good routine:** on the 5th of each month, after pension arrives, sit with your notebook. Pay each bill, write the amount and reference number, and tick it off. This turns a list of errands that once meant four queues into ten quiet minutes.

**Reading your history.** Every app has a 'History' or 'Transactions' page. Once a week, scroll through it with a cup of tea. Every line should be something you remember. Anything strange? Call your bank the same day.

left.title: Cash in the wallet
points: No record unless you write it
No PIN needed by a thief

sections.md:
Act fast — the first hours matter.

1. **Call 1930**, the national cyber-crime helpline, or report at **cybercrime.gov.in**. They can try to freeze the money while it is still moving.
2. **Call your bank** using the number on your passbook, card or the bank's official website — not a number from Google search results or an SMS. Ask them to block UPI.
3. **Change your UPI PIN** if you think anyone saw it.
4. Keep screenshots and the transaction ID.
5. Tell your family. There is no shame — clever, educated people are cheated every day by professional criminals. Speaking up protects others.

Digital payments are now part of Indian life, like the railway reservation counter once was. With the golden rule and the five checks, you can enjoy them with confidence.

check.q: Money was taken by fraud. Which number should you call first in India?
check.why: 1930 is the national cyber-crime helpline, which can try to stop stolen money quickly.

story.title: Kamala Aunty and the Sofa Buyer

parts.md: Kamala Iyer, seventy-two, retired headmistress of a Chennai girls' school, decided the old teak sofa had to go. Her son in Bengaluru put it online for ₹9,000. Within an hour her phone rang. 'Madam, I am Captain Rajesh, just transferred to Avadi. Your sofa is perfect. I will pay full amount, no bargaining.' He was so polite that Kamala smiled. 'I am sending payment request,' he said. 'Just enter your PIN and the money will come to you.'

A notification arrived: *Rajesh K is requesting ₹9,000.* Below it, a bright button: **Pay**. Kamala's thumb hovered. Something old and schoolteacherly stirred in her. *Request… pay… why would I pay to receive?* She remembered the line from her grandson's lesson: **PIN means money going out.** 'Captain,' she said sweetly, 'please send it the normal way, to my number. I don't need to press anything to receive, no?'

The captain's voice changed. 'Madam, system problem, only request works, hurry or I go to another seller.' Kamala declined the request, blocked the number and called her son. Then she dialled 1930 and reported it, just as the read had said. The next week a real buyer came, a young couple, who paid by scanning her QR code while she did nothing at all. *Received nine thousand rupees*, announced her phone. Kamala laughed. 'Lesson learned, lesson taught,' she told the couple, and gave them her recipe for filter coffee too.

summary: UPI moves money directly between bank accounts; the app is only a window.
A UPI ID looks like name@bank; a QR code is a UPI ID as a picture.
The PIN is needed only to send money (and to check balance yourself) — never to receive.
Set up using your bank-registered mobile number and debit card or Aadhaar OTP.
Always check payee name and amount before entering the PIN; try a ₹1 test with new payees.
Decline unknown collect requests and 'scan to receive' QR codes.
Never install screen-sharing apps at a caller's request.
Scams use hurry, fear or greed — Stop, Think, Check.
No police agency arrests anyone over a video call.
Use a separate low-balance account, daily limits and app lock.
Failed transactions are usually reversed automatically; raise a dispute if not.
Pay bills via BBPS, note reference numbers, and review history weekly.
Report fraud on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in immediately; consult your bank for account questions.

glossary.d: Unified Payments Interface — India's instant bank-to-bank payment system
National Payments Corporation of India, which runs UPI
A request asking you to approve paying money
Bharat BillPay System for paying utility bills
Unique Transaction Reference — the receipt number of a payment
A small pre-loaded balance for quick low-value payments without PIN

rd-seniors-video-calls.title: Video Calls with Family
rd-seniors-video-calls.subtitle: See your grandchildren's faces from across the country — or the world — every Sunday

sections.h: A window instead of a letter
sections.md:
Kamala ji's son moved to Toronto in 2009. For years their link was a phone call every Sunday, crackling and expensive, where she would ask, 'Have you eaten?' and he would always say yes. Then her niece set up a video call. On the screen appeared her son's kitchen, a pot of dal on the stove, and a toddler in pyjamas waving a toy elephant. 'That's your Dadi,' her son said. Kamala ji cried, and laughed, and has not missed a Sunday since.

A video call is simply a phone call where you also see each other, using the internet instead of the ordinary phone line. On WhatsApp, Google Meet, or Apple FaceTime it costs nothing extra beyond your data or Wi‑Fi — even to America or Australia.

This read shows you how to make and receive video calls, how to join a meeting from a link, how to look and sound good, how to manage group calls with the whole family, how to save data, how to make calls easier for tired eyes and ears, and how to fix the small troubles that always arise.

- A smartphone (or tablet or laptop) with a **front camera** — the small dot above the screen.
- **Internet**: home Wi‑Fi is best. Mobile data works too; a 30-minute video call uses very roughly a few hundred MB, depending on quality.
- An app: **WhatsApp** (most Indian families), **Google Meet**, **FaceTime** (iPhone to iPhone), or **Zoom** (for larger meetings or satsang groups).
- The other person's number saved in your contacts.

Optional but lovely: a small **phone stand** (₹150–₹300 at any mobile shop) so you don't hold the phone for half an hour, and **wired or Bluetooth earphones** if hearing is difficult or the house is noisy.

**Tablet or phone?** A tablet's bigger screen is wonderful for group calls where six faces share the screen. A phone is handier for walking around and showing the house. Many seniors keep a tablet on a stand in the drawing room just for the Sunday call.

**Saving a contact properly** makes calling easier: open Contacts → ➕ → type the name the way you think of the person ('Beta Anil Toronto', 'Pinky Dubai') with the country code (+1, +971). Once saved, the person appears in WhatsApp automatically.

check.q: Which connection usually gives the smoothest video call at home?
check.why: Home Wi‑Fi is generally faster and steadier than mobile data, and doesn't use up your data pack.

sections.md:
**One person:**

1. Open WhatsApp.
2. Tap the chat with the person (e.g. 'Beta Anil').
3. At the top right you'll see a 📞 phone and a 📹 camera icon. Tap the **camera**.
4. Wait while it rings. When they answer, their face fills the screen and yours appears in a small box.
5. To end, tap the **red** button.

**Receiving:** when someone video-calls, the screen lights up with their name. **Swipe up** or tap the green button to answer.

**Buttons during a call** (tap the screen once if they disappear):

- 🎤 microphone — tap to mute yourself (useful if the pressure cooker whistles!)
- 📹 camera — turn your video off and on
- 🔄 flip — switch to the back camera to *show* things: your garden, the new curtains, the Diwali rangoli
- 🔊 speaker — louder sound

**Missed a call?** WhatsApp shows a missed-call line in the chat. Tap the 📹 beside it to call back. If you are not ready — still in the kitchen — send a quick message 'Call in 10 min 🙏' instead.

**Switching from voice to video.** If you are already on a normal WhatsApp voice call and want to show something, tap the camera button during the call; the other person gets a request to switch on video.

check.q: You want to show your grandson the mango tree outside. Which button helps?
check.why: Flip switches to the back camera so the other person sees what you are pointing at.

sections.h: Joining a Google Meet or Zoom from a link
sections.md:
Sometimes the family, a satsang group, your alumni association or a doctor's clinic sends a **link** instead of calling. It looks like `meet.google.com/abc-defg-hij` or `zoom.us/j/123456789`. Joining is easier than it looks.

**Google Meet:**

1. Tap the blue link in WhatsApp or SMS.
2. If asked, open it in the **Meet** app (install from Play Store once) or in Chrome.
3. You see a preview of your own face. Check the 🎤 and 📹 are on.
4. Tap **Join** or **Ask to join**. The organiser lets you in.

**Zoom:**

1. Tap the link; install the **Zoom Workplace** app if prompted (publisher: Zoom).
2. Type your name as you'd like it shown — 'Sharma Uncle (Jaipur)' helps everyone.
3. Tap **Join with video**, then **Join audio → Call via device audio**. Forgetting this last step is the most common reason people 'can't hear anything' in Zoom.
4. Some meetings need a **passcode**; it is usually in the same message as the link.

**Leaving:** tap the red **Leave** button. In a big meeting, staying muted until you want to speak is good manners — and saves embarrassment if the doorbell rings.
keyTerms: Link — a web address you tap to join a meeting
Host — the person who runs the meeting and lets people in
Passcode — a short code needed to enter some meetings

check.q: In Zoom you see everyone but hear nothing. What is the likely fix?
options: Tap Join audio → Call via device audio
check.why: Zoom keeps sound off until you choose 'Join audio', so tapping it connects your speaker and microphone.

sections.h: FaceTime and video calls on iPhones
sections.md:
If you and your family both use iPhones or iPads, **FaceTime** is already on the device — no download.

1. Open the green **FaceTime** app, or open the person in Contacts.
2. Tap the 📹 **video** icon next to their name.
3. Buttons look similar: mute, camera off, flip, and red to end.

FaceTime also lets an iPhone user send a **FaceTime link** to someone with an Android phone or a computer; the other person can join through the web browser. Ask your family to 'send me a FaceTime link' if they prefer FaceTime.

Most Indian families, though, use **WhatsApp video**, because it works the same on Android and iPhone. If in doubt, use WhatsApp — everyone in the family can help you with it.

sections.h: Group calls: the whole family on one screen
sections.md:
Festivals are perfect for group calls — Diwali in Delhi, Bangalore and Dubai at once.

**On WhatsApp:**

- Open the family **group** and tap the 📹 icon — it will ring everyone (WhatsApp allows a fairly large group; check the current limit in the app).
- Or start a call with one person, then tap **Add participant** ➕ to add others.

The screen divides into boxes, one per person. When many people talk together it becomes noisy, so try a little 'call etiquette':

- One person speaks at a time; others mute.
- Children often love to show a drawing or perform a song — give them a turn.
- Plan a time in advance across time zones. 8 pm in India is 9:30 am in Toronto (in winter) — check before fixing.

For larger gatherings like a 75th birthday with 40 relatives, **Google Meet** or **Zoom** with a link shared in the family group works well. A grandchild can be the 'host'.

**Working out the time.** India is 5½ hours ahead of London in winter. So 8:00 pm in India minus 5:30 is 2:30 pm in London. Dubai is 1½ hours behind India: 8:00 pm − 1:30 = 6:30 pm. Singapore is 2½ hours ahead: 8:00 pm + 2:30 = 10:30 pm.

head: City
When it's 8:00 pm in India
Note
rows: 1:30 am next day (Australian summer) / 12:30 am (Australian winter)
Better to call in your morning
fig.caption: Approximate time differences — India does not change clocks, but many countries do. Double-check with family.

check.q: It is 7:00 pm in India. What time is it in Dubai?
check.why: Dubai is 1½ hours behind India, so 7:00 pm − 1:30 = 5:30 pm.

sections.md:
A few small tricks make calls far more pleasant for both sides:

- **Light in front, not behind.** Sit facing a window or lamp. If the window is behind you, you become a dark silhouette.
- **Camera at eye level.** Rest the phone on a stand or a stack of books. Holding it low shows mainly your chin and the ceiling fan!
- **Hold it steady**, or better, don't hold it.
- **Quiet corner.** Switch off the TV; close the window if traffic is loud.
- **Glasses on**, hearing aid in, and volume up before the call.
- **Look at the camera dot** sometimes, not only the screen — it feels like eye contact to the other person.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#f7f3ea'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' fill='#333'><text x='60' y='30'>❌ Window behind</text><text x='370' y='30'>✅ Light in front</text></g><rect x='40' y='45' width='220' height='180' fill='#fffbe0'/><circle cx='150' cy='130' r='45' fill='#333'/><rect x='95' y='170' width='110' height='55' fill='#333'/><rect x='340' y='45' width='220' height='180' fill='#dfe9f5'/><circle cx='450' cy='130' r='45' fill='#e8b48a'><animate attributeName='fill' values='#7a5a44;#e8b48a;#e8b48a' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><rect x='395' y='170' width='110' height='55' fill='#4a7bd0'/><circle cx='450' cy='-10' r='30' fill='#ffd34d'><animate attributeName='cy' values='-10;20;20' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><path d='M450 50 L450 80 M425 55 L435 80 M475 55 L465 80' stroke='#f5b400' stroke-width='3'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;1;1' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path></svg>
fig.caption: With a bright window behind you, your face goes dark; turn round so the light falls on your face.
fig.alt: Two pictures: a dark silhouette against a window, and a brightly lit face facing a lamp.

sections.md:
Ageing eyes and ears need not keep you from calls. Phones have helpers built in:

- **Bigger text and buttons:** Settings → Display → Font size and Display size. WhatsApp follows these.
- **Hearing aids:** many modern hearing aids connect to the phone by **Bluetooth**, so the caller's voice goes straight into your ears. Ask your audiologist to pair them.
- **Live Caption:** on many Android phones (Settings → Accessibility → Live Caption) and on iPhones (Live Captions), the phone writes on screen, in English, what the other person is saying. Google Meet has its own **CC** button for captions, including several Indian languages in some regions.
- **Answer by voice:** you can ask Google Assistant or Siri, 'Video call Anil on WhatsApp', if your fingers are stiff.
- **Stand and charger nearby:** a call can use battery quickly; keep the charger plugged in near your chair.

None of this is cheating. Your grandchildren use glasses for screens too!

check.q: You find it hard to follow fast speech on Google Meet. Which feature helps?
check.why: Captions turn the speaker's words into text on your screen as they talk.

sections.md:
On Wi‑Fi you need not worry. On a mobile data pack, video calls can eat data. Rough guide: a normal WhatsApp video call uses several megabytes per minute; an hour can use roughly half a gigabyte or more, depending on quality. If your daily pack is 1.5 GB, one long call is fine, but three may finish it.

Tips:

- In WhatsApp: Settings → **Storage and data** → *Use less data for calls*.
- Ask family to call when you are on **home Wi‑Fi**.
- Switch off your own video for a while (keep listening) if the network is weak — sound needs much less data than pictures.
- Check your remaining data in your operator's app (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL).

If the picture keeps freezing, it is usually a network issue, not your fault and not your phone's.

Every caller faces these. Here is your troubleshooting table — keep it near the phone. If nothing works, end the call, wait a minute, and call again; this simple restart solves a surprising number of problems.

head: Problem
Try this
rows: Check 🎤 isn't muted (no line through it); remove phone cover blocking mic
Press volume up during the call; tap 🔊 speaker
Move closer to the Wi‑Fi router; ask others at home to pause downloads
Switch between Wi‑Fi and mobile data; restart the phone
Check 📹 isn't switched off; clean the camera lens with a soft cloth
Rest it on a hard surface; end and call again later
Ask the other person to lower speaker volume or use earphones
fig.caption: Ninety percent of troubles are solved by one of these steps.

check.q: Your face appears very dark on the call. What's the likely cause?
check.why: Strong light behind you makes the camera darken your face; sit facing the light instead.

sections.md:
Video calls with family are safe. But be careful with calls from **unknown numbers**:

- **Do not answer video calls from numbers you don't know**, especially international ones. Some criminals record such calls and use them for blackmail, or pretend to be police ('digital arrest' scam — see our scam-safety read). No real police agency questions or arrests anyone over a video call.
- In WhatsApp: Settings → Privacy → Calls → **Silence unknown callers**.
- Never show your Aadhaar, bank card, cheque book or passbook on a video call.
- Don't share your screen with anyone except family you can see and trust.
- If someone you know calls asking for money urgently, call them back on their usual number, or ask your family code word. Voices and even faces can now be faked with computer tools.
- If you are cheated or threatened, call **1930** or report at cybercrime.gov.in.

With these simple habits, the video call becomes what it should be — a window into the lives of the people you love.

check.q: An unknown international number video-calls you. Best action?
check.why: Unknown video calls are a common route for blackmail and impersonation scams.

sections.md:
Technology is only half the story. The other half is habit. Families that stay close across distance often keep a fixed slot: *Sunday 11 am, Dadi's call.*

Ideas to make calls richer:

- **Story time**: read a Panchatantra tale to a grandchild before bed in their time zone.
- **Cook-along**: teach your famous rajma recipe while your daughter cooks in her kitchen.
- **Homework helper**: many retired teachers and engineers help grandchildren with maths over video.
- **Show and tell**: old photo albums, a new plant, the first mango of summer.
- **Pooja or aarti** together on festival days.
- **Antakshari**: a family song game works beautifully over a group call.

A ten-minute call with full attention is worth more than an hour of distracted talk. Put away other things, smile, and enjoy.

> Did you know? Many families now 'eat together' over video — the phone propped on the dining table at dinner time, two kitchens connected for half an hour.

parts.md: Prakash Mehta of Vadodara was turning eighty, and his granddaughter Riya in Singapore announced a surprise: a Zoom party with forty relatives from four countries. Prakash had made WhatsApp calls for years, but Zoom sounded like a racing car. At 6:55 pm he tapped the link Riya had sent. A screen asked for his name. He typed, slowly, 'PRAKASH 80'. Then — nothing. Faces appeared, mouths moved, but the room was silent.

His heart sank. Was the phone broken? Then he remembered Riya's voice note: *'Dadu, after joining, press Join audio.'* At the bottom of the screen he found it, pressed **Call via device audio**, and the drawing room filled with forty people singing 'Happy Birthday' slightly out of time, his sister in Leicester the loudest of all. He laughed so hard his glasses fell off.

Later, during antakshari, his nephew in New Jersey's sound kept echoing. Prakash, now the expert, unmuted himself and said, 'Beta, use your earphones!' The echo vanished. At the end Riya said, 'Dadu, next year you host.' He wrote in his diary that night: *Eighty years old, and I learnt a new button.*

summary: A video call shows both faces using the internet, at no extra cost beyond data/Wi‑Fi.
You need a front camera, internet and an app like WhatsApp, Meet, FaceTime or Zoom.
WhatsApp: open chat → tap 📹; swipe up to answer; red to end.
Buttons: mute, camera off, flip, speaker.
Meet/Zoom: tap the link, check mic and camera, Join; in Zoom tap Join audio.
Group calls: tap 📹 in a group or add participants; one person speaks at a time.
Mind time zones; many countries change clocks seasonally.
Face the light; keep the camera at eye level on a stand.
Use bigger text, Bluetooth hearing aids and captions if needed.
Save data with 'use less data for calls' and Wi‑Fi.
Most problems: check mute, volume, Wi‑Fi, permissions, restart.
Don't answer unknown video calls; silence unknown callers; report threats on 1930.
Make calls a weekly family ritual with stories, cooking and show-and-tell.
practice: Make a WhatsApp video call to a family member and use the flip button.
Join a Google Meet from a link a family member sends you.
Set up a group video call with three relatives.
List three ways to look better on camera.
What would you check if the other person cannot hear you?
Work out what time it is in Dubai when it is 7 pm in India, and in Singapore.
Turn on 'Silence unknown callers' and 'Use less data for calls' in WhatsApp.
Find and try Live Caption on your phone.
Plan a weekly family video ritual and write it down.

rd-stories-boondi-raindrop.title: Boondi the Little Raindrop
rd-stories-boondi-raindrop.subtitle: A raindrop's journey from the sea to a Mumbai window and back again — the water cycle as a bedtime story.

sections.md:
Have you ever watched raindrops race down a window? Tonight's story is about one of them — a little drop called **Boondi**.

Boondi lives in the big blue Arabian Sea near Mumbai. One hot day, something magical happens to her, and she goes on the longest journey of her life: up into the sky, across the land, down a mountain, deep under the ground, and home again.

Grown-ups: this story quietly teaches the **water cycle**. Point at the picture as Boondi travels. The story is long enough for two nights — stop after the sparrow on the first night if eyes are closing.

- Where did Boondi live at the start? Where did she end up?
- What made Boondi float up into the sky?
- What did Boondi help on her journey? (The farmer's rice, the thirsty sparrow, the village well, the little girl's paper boat.)
- How did Boondi feel when she was deep under the ground? What helped her be brave?

**Did you know?** The water you drink today might once have been a raindrop over a dinosaur! Water on Earth goes round and round, again and again.

check.q: What made Boondi rise up from the sea?
check.why: When the Sun warms water, tiny bits of it turn into invisible vapour and float up — this is called evaporation.

sections.md:
Boondi's journey has four big words that scientists use. Say them slowly together, like a song:

| Big word | What it means | In the story |
|---|---|---|
| **Evaporation** (ee-vap-o-RAY-shun) | Warm water turns into invisible vapour and rises | Boondi floats off the wave |
| **Condensation** (con-den-SAY-shun) | Cool vapour turns back into tiny drops | Drops huddle into a cloud |
| **Precipitation** (pre-sip-i-TAY-shun) | Drops fall from clouds as rain (or hail or snow) | The first monsoon rain |
| **Collection** | Water gathers in rivers, lakes, under the ground and the sea | The well, the river, home to Lehar |

A fun way to remember: *Up, huddle, down, home!* Wave your arms up for evaporation, hug yourself for condensation, wiggle your fingers down for rain, and swoosh your hands sideways for the river going home.

check.q: When drops huddle together high in the cool sky, what do they make?
check.why: Cooling vapour turns back into tiny drops that crowd together into a cloud — this is condensation.

sections.h: Try it at home (with a grown-up)
sections.md:
**1. Make a cloud in a cup.** Fill a steel tumbler with ice cubes. Wait five minutes. Tiny drops appear on the outside! Water vapour in the air touched the cold steel and turned back into drops — just like Boondi meeting the cool sky.

**2. Watch water disappear.** Put two spoons of water on a plate in the sun and two on a plate in the shade. Which dries first? The sunny one — the Sun helps water evaporate, the way it lifted Boondi.

**3. Mini water cycle.** A grown-up pours warm (not hot) water into a glass bowl and covers it tightly with cling film. Put an ice cube on top of the film. Soon, drops form under the film and drip down like rain.

**4. Save Boondi's friends.** Turn off the tap while brushing your teeth. Use a bucket instead of a running pipe to wash the scooter. Every drop saved is a drop for a rice plant or a sparrow.

> Did you know? In many Indian villages people build little ponds and wells to catch monsoon rain so there is water all year. This is called **rainwater harvesting**.

parts.md:
In the big, blue Arabian Sea, near the city of Mumbai, there lived a tiny drop of water called **Boondi**.

Boondi was so small you could not see her all by herself. She lived with millions and millions of other drops, all squished together, rolling in the waves. *Whoosh* went the waves up the sandy beach. *Shhhh* went the waves back again.

Boondi loved the sea. She played with the silver fish. She rode on the backs of the waves like a child on a swing. She tickled the toes of children building sandcastles at Juhu beach.

But sometimes Boondi looked up at the sky and wondered.

"What is it like up there?" she asked her friend, an old wise wave called **Lehar**. "Up where the seagulls fly? Up where the clouds float?"

Lehar laughed a frothy laugh. "One day you'll find out, little Boondi. Every drop goes on a journey. When the Sun decides it is time."

"When will that be?"

"Be patient," said Lehar. "The Sun is always watching."

Summer came. It was hot — very, very hot. The sand on the beach was too hot to walk on. People in Mumbai fanned themselves and drank cold nimbu-pani. The street dogs lay in the shade with their tongues out.

And the Sun shone down on the sea, bright and golden and warm.

Boondi was floating right at the top of a wave, sunbathing. She felt warmer, and warmer, and warmer. And then she felt something strange.

She felt... *light*.

Lighter than a feather. Lighter than a soap bubble. So light that she lifted right off the top of the wave!

"Lehar!" she cried. "I'm floating! I'm flying!"

"Goodbye, Boondi!" called the old wave. "Have a wonderful journey! Come home soon!"

Boondi had turned into **vapour** — so tiny and so light that she was invisible, like your breath on a warm day. Up she went, past the fishing boats, past the seagulls, past the tall buildings of the city, up and up into the blue sky.

*Can you float up like Boondi? Lift your arms up, up, up!*

Up in the sky, it was cool. Much cooler than the beach. Boondi shivered.

And as she cooled down, she bumped into another tiny drop. And another. And another.

"Hello!" they said. "Come and join us!"

The drops held hands and huddled together to keep warm. More and more drops came floating up from the sea, until there were so many of them, all snuggled close, that they made something white and fluffy.

They made a **cloud**.

Boondi was part of a cloud! She could hardly believe it. She looked down and saw the whole coastline of India spread out below her like a map — the blue sea, the brown beaches, the green fields, and far away, the dark hills of the Western Ghats.

Then a big wind came. It was the **monsoon wind**, and it blew from the sea towards the land, as it does every June.

"All aboard!" it whooshed. "Next stop: the mountains!"

And the whole cloud, with Boondi inside it, sailed off across the sky.

On the way, the cloud passed a kite — not a paper kite, but a real bird, a big brown **cheel** with wide wings, gliding in circles.

"Where are you all going in such a hurry?" asked the cheel, tilting her head.

"To the mountains!" sang the drops. "The monsoon wind is taking us."

"Then hold on tight," said the cheel. "Down below, the whole land is waiting for you. The ponds are cracked. The wells are low. The frogs have been asleep in the mud for months, dreaming of rain."

Boondi peeped over the edge of the cloud. It was true. The fields were brown and dusty. A little pond looked like an empty plate. A boy was pulling a bucket from a well, and it came up only half full.

"Everyone is waiting for us?" Boondi asked.

"Everyone," said the cheel. "You are small, but together you are the monsoon."

Boondi felt very important, and a little bit nervous, and very, very excited.

The cloud floated over villages and fields. More clouds joined it, until the sky was full of great grey clouds, rumbling and grumbling.

Then they came to the mountains — the tall, green Western Ghats. The clouds had to climb up, up, over the hills. And the higher they went, the colder it got.

Boondi felt herself getting heavier. All the drops around her were getting heavier too. They were bumping together and growing fatter and rounder.

"I can't stay up any more!" said one drop.

"Neither can I!" said another.

And then — *rumble, rumble, CRASH!* went the thunder. *Flash!* went the lightning.

And Boondi fell.

Down, down, down she tumbled, with millions of other raindrops, *pitter-patter-pitter-patter*, out of the sky.

It was the **first rain of the monsoon**!

Below, in a little village, a farmer named **Ramu Kaka** looked up and laughed with joy. "The rains are here!" he shouted. Children ran out and danced. The dry brown earth gave off a lovely smell, the smell of rain on hot soil. And in the pond, the frogs woke up and sang, *trrr-trrr, trrr-trrr!*

Boondi landed — *plip!* — on a tiny green rice plant in Ramu Kaka's field.

The rice plant had been so thirsty. Its leaves were dry and curling.

"Oh, thank you," whispered the rice plant, as Boondi slid down its leaf and soaked into the soil by its roots. "Now I can grow tall and give rice to the farmer's family."

Boondi felt warm and happy inside. She had helped!

But she didn't stay in the soil for long. She trickled through the earth, joining other drops, until she came out into a little stream. The stream was chattering and gurgling down the hill.

On a rock beside the stream sat a small brown **sparrow**. She was hot and dusty from the long summer.

Boondi splashed up onto the rock, and the sparrow dipped her beak and took a sip.

"Mmm," said the sparrow. "Fresh, cool rain water. That's just what I needed."

*Who has Boondi helped so far? The rice plant... and the sparrow!*

The stream wiggled past a mango tree, and at its roots there was a little crack in the ground. Boondi slipped — *shloop!* — into the crack.

Down she went, into the dark. Through soft soil. Between little stones. Past the curly roots of the mango tree. Past a sleepy earthworm, who opened one eye and said, "Mind your step, little drop."

It was very dark and very quiet. Boondi felt a tiny bit scared.

"Hello?" she whispered.

"Hello!" answered many soft voices. All around her, in the sand and gravel deep underground, there were drops, drops, drops — resting quietly, like children asleep in a big dormitory.

"Who are you?" Boondi asked.

"We are the **groundwater**," said an old drop. "We rest here under the earth. In the dry months, people dig wells and pull us up to drink and cook. We are the village's secret treasure."

Boondi was not scared any more. She was with friends. And she knew that in the dark, under the ground, drops were keeping a promise to the people above.

Boondi rested for a while. Then, slowly, slowly, she seeped along through the sand until she came to a round stone wall. It was the inside of the **village well**!

Above her, a circle of sky. A rope came down, and a bucket went *splash!* Boondi tumbled in with lots of other drops, and up, up, up the bucket rose.

At the top was **Meena**, Ramu Kaka's daughter. She poured the water into a clay matka to keep it cool.

That evening, after working in the field all day, Ramu Kaka came home tired and hot. Meena filled a steel tumbler from the matka and held it out.

"Thank you, beti," he said, and drank. "Ahh. Sweet monsoon water."

Boondi did not stay in the tumbler — a few drops splashed onto the floor and ran out of the door, down the lane and into the little stream again. But she was glad. She had cooled a tired farmer at the end of a long day.

*Rice plant, sparrow, farmer... who will Boondi help next?*

The little stream joined a bigger stream. The bigger stream joined a **river**. Boondi rushed along, past villages and temples and banyan trees, past buffaloes cooling off in the water and women washing bright saris on the steps.

The river flowed all the way back towards Mumbai. It was raining in the city too — great curtains of rain. The streets were full of puddles. People hurried under umbrellas, black and red and yellow.

At the edge of a big puddle near a school, a little girl named **Tara** was kneeling down. She had folded a boat out of a page from her notebook.

"Go, little boat!" she said, and put it on the water.

Boondi was in that puddle. She rushed forward with the other drops and pushed the paper boat along — *whoosh!* — round a stone, past a leaf, all the way to the other side.

"It's sailing!" cried Tara, clapping her hands. "Look, Mamma, it's sailing!"

Boondi wiggled with happiness. She had made a little girl laugh.

From the puddle, Boondi trickled into a drain, and from the drain into a big river that wound through the city, and from the river — at last — out, out, into the wide blue sea.

*Whoosh* went the waves. *Shhhh.*

"Boondi!" called a frothy, familiar voice. "Is that you?"

It was Lehar, the old wise wave!

"Lehar!" cried Boondi. "I'm home! I went up into the sky and I became a cloud and I rode on the monsoon wind and I fell as rain on the mountains!"

"And what did you do there?" asked Lehar.

"I gave a drink to a thirsty rice plant," said Boondi. "And to a dusty sparrow. I slept under the ground with the groundwater, and came up in a well for a tired farmer. And I sailed a little girl's paper boat!"

Lehar smiled. "That is what every drop does. We go up, we come down, we help along the way, and we come home again. Round and round, for ever and ever. It is called the **water cycle**."

"Round and round," said Boondi sleepily. "Will I go again?"

"Oh yes. Whenever the Sun says it is time."

Night came over the Arabian Sea. The Sun went down in a blaze of orange and pink, and a silver moon came up.

The waves grew gentle. *Whoosh... shhhh... whoosh... shhhh...*

Boondi snuggled in among her millions of friends. She was tired after her big journey — tired in the good way, like after a whole day of playing.

Far away, in a village under the mountains, a little rice plant was already a tiny bit taller. A sparrow was asleep in her nest. The frogs were still singing in the full pond. Meena's matka stood cool in the corner. And in a house in Mumbai, a girl named Tara had put her wet paper boat on the windowsill to dry, so she could sail it again tomorrow.

Outside Tara's window, the rain was still falling softly. *Pitter-patter. Pitter-patter.*

Maybe, Tara thought as she fell asleep, one of those raindrops was the very same one that pushed my boat.

And maybe it was.

*Whoosh... shhhh... whoosh... shhhh...*

Goodnight, Boondi. Goodnight, Lehar. Goodnight, Tara.

*Goodnight, little one.*

summary: Boondi is a tiny water drop in the Arabian Sea near Mumbai.
The hot Sun warms her and she rises as invisible vapour (evaporation).
High in the cool sky, drops join up to make a cloud (condensation).
The monsoon wind blows the cloud to the Western Ghats; a cheel tells her the land is waiting.
Drops grow heavy and fall as rain (precipitation).
Boondi helps a rice plant and a sparrow.
She sinks underground and rests as groundwater, then comes up in a village well for Ramu Kaka.
She sails Tara's paper boat in a Mumbai puddle.
Streams and rivers carry her back to the sea — the water cycle goes round and round.

It is **Diwali** night in a small house in Lucknow. Everyone is busy: Mummy is making rangoli, Papa is hanging lights, and Nani is frying crispy mathris.

Under the bed, in the toy box, lives **Chhotu Chhuk-Chhuk** — a small red wooden train with three carriages and a bell that goes *ting-ting*. Tonight, Chhotu has a very important job.

Grown-ups: join in with *chhuk-chhuk-chhuk* and *ting-ting!* each time the train moves. Let your child count the friends who help Chhotu — there are five.

sections.md:
Diwali (also called **Deepavali**, which means *a row of lamps*) is one of India's biggest festivals. It comes in autumn, usually in October or November, on the darkest night of the month — the new-moon night of the month of Kartik.

Different families tell different stories about Diwali:

- Many remember **Lord Rama** coming home to Ayodhya after fourteen years, when people lit lamps to welcome him.
- Many pray to **Goddess Lakshmi** for a happy, healthy year.
- **Jain** families remember Lord Mahavira, and **Sikh** families celebrate **Bandi Chhor Divas** on the same days.

What do people do? They clean their homes, draw **rangoli** at the door, light **diyas**, wear new clothes, share **mithai** with neighbours, and visit family. In Lucknow, like Arjun's family, many people also make crispy **mathris** and sweet **gujiyas**.

The big idea of Diwali is simple enough for the smallest child: *light beats darkness, kindness beats sadness, and we are happiest when we share.*

check.q: What does 'Deepavali' mean?
check.why: 'Deep' means lamp and 'avali' means a row, so Deepavali is a row of lamps.

sections.md:
Chhotu learnt two safety lessons on his journey: go *around* the slippery oil, and stay calm when the loud noises come. Here are some Diwali safety rules for real children:

- 🪔 **Diyas are hot.** Never touch the flame. Keep diyas away from curtains, dupattas and paper.
- 👗 Wear **cotton clothes** near lamps and sparklers; flowing synthetic clothes can catch fire.
- 🧑‍🧒 Light sparklers only with a **grown-up**, in an open space, with a **bucket of water** nearby.
- 🐕 Animals like dogs, cats and birds get scared of loud noise. Many families choose **quiet, green celebrations** with lights, rangoli and music instead of loud crackers.
- 👂 If loud sounds scare you, cover your ears or hold a grown-up's hand. It's okay to feel scared — Chhotu did too!

> Did you know? Clay diyas are made by potters on a spinning wheel. Buying diyas from local potters helps them celebrate Diwali too.

right.title: Don't 🚫
points: Touch a flame or a hot diya
Throw crackers near animals or people

parts.md:
It was Diwali in a little yellow house in Lucknow.

The whole house smelled of ghee and cardamom and marigold flowers. Mummy was on the floor of the courtyard, making a big rangoli with coloured powder — pink, orange, green and blue — in the shape of a lotus. Papa was standing on a stool, hanging a string of tiny twinkling lights. And Nani was in the kitchen, frying mathris that went *sizzle-sizzle* in the pan.

A little boy named **Arjun** was helping. He put out the diyas in a long row along the doorstep. One, two, three, four... ten little clay lamps.

"Nani," said Arjun, "where's *your* diya? The blue one?"

Nani's special diya was painted blue with white dots, like stars. Her own mother had given it to her, a long time ago, when Nani was a little girl. Every Diwali, Nani lit it first.

Nani looked on the shelf. She looked in the cupboard. She looked in the puja box.

"Oh dear," she said softly. "I can't find it."

She smiled, but her eyes looked a little bit sad.

And under the bed, inside the toy box, somebody heard.

Inside the toy box lived **Chhotu Chhuk-Chhuk**.

Chhotu was a small red wooden train. He had a black chimney, three carriages — red, blue and green — and a little brass bell that went *ting-ting*. Arjun had had him since he was a baby.

And lying right next to Chhotu, in the corner of the toy box, was something round and blue with white dots.

Nani's diya!

It must have rolled off the shelf and under the bed and *plop* into the toy box when Arjun was tidying up.

"Oh!" said Chhotu. "Nani needs this. And the lamps will be lit when the first star comes out. I must take it to her!"

But Chhotu was only a little toy train. The toy box had a lid. The bed was low. And the doorstep was very, very far away — all the way down the hallway, through the kitchen, to the front door.

Chhotu rang his bell bravely. *Ting-ting!*

"I can do it," he said. "Chhuk-chhuk-chhuk. One wheel at a time."

First, Chhotu had to get out of the toy box.

He pushed against the lid. It didn't move. He pushed harder. *Ting-ting!* It still didn't move.

"Need some help, little engine?"

It was **Bhalu**, the big brown teddy bear, with one button eye and one stitched eye and a red bow tie.

"Bhalu! I have to take Nani's diya to the doorstep before the first star!"

"Then up we go," said Bhalu. He stood up on his soft fluffy legs, put his paws against the lid, and pushed. *Creeeak!* The lid opened.

Bhalu lifted the blue diya and placed it carefully in Chhotu's middle carriage. Then he lifted Chhotu out and set him on the floor.

"Thank you, Bhalu!"

"Go safely," said Bhalu, waving his paw. "Chhuk-chhuk!"

Chhotu rolled out from under the bed into the bedroom. *Chhuk-chhuk-chhuk.* The floor was smooth and cool. Through the window, the sky was turning from orange to purple.

*Not long now until the first star!*

Chhotu rolled to the bedroom door and into the long hallway. But the hallway had a rug — a thick, fluffy rug — and Chhotu's little wheels got stuck in it.

*Chhuk... chhuk... chh...* He couldn't move!

"Oh no," said Chhotu. "I'm stuck, and the diya might fall out!"

"Hold on!" called a small voice from the shelf.

It was **Rani**, the rag doll, with yarn plaits and a bright patchwork lehenga. She slid down the leg of the table and ran over.

"I know what to do," said Rani. She untied the long golden ribbon from her plait. She tied one end to the front of Chhotu's engine, and held the other end in both hands.

"Ready? One, two, three — PULL!"

Rani pulled. Chhotu pushed his wheels round as hard as he could. And slowly, slowly, he rolled over the fluffy rug and onto the smooth floor on the other side.

"You did it!" said Rani.

"*We* did it," said Chhotu. *Ting-ting!*

Rani tied her ribbon back in her hair. "Hurry now. I can hear Papa saying it's nearly time!"

At the end of the hallway was the kitchen. And between the hallway and the kitchen was a **step**.

To you, it would be a tiny step. But to a little toy train, it was like a cliff.

Chhotu peered over the edge. "How do I get down without the diya breaking?"

A pair of whiskers poked out from behind the cupboard. Then a pink nose. Then two shiny black eyes.

It was **Ginni**, a little grey mouse who lived in the house. (Nani pretended not to know about her, and sometimes left a crumb of mathri by the cupboard, just in case.)

"Follow me," squeaked Ginni. "There's a secret way. Nani's rolling board leans against the step. It makes a slide!"

Sure enough, there was the flat wooden board Nani used for rolling chapatis, propped against the step like a ramp.

"Slowly, now," said Ginni.

Chhotu took a deep breath. *Ting-ting.* And very slowly, wheels squeaking, he rolled down the rolling board — *chhuk... chhuk... chhuk* — all the way to the kitchen floor. The blue diya didn't wobble once.

"Thank you, Ginni!"

"Thank *you*," said Ginni. "Nani is always kind to me. I want her to have a happy Diwali."

Chhotu was in a hurry now. *Chhuk-chhuk-chhuk-chhuk!* He rolled faster and faster across the kitchen floor.

But right in front of him, shining in the light, was a little golden puddle. When Nani had filled the diyas, a few drops of **oil** had spilled on the floor.

"Stop! Stop!" squeaked Ginni from behind him.

Chhotu squeezed his brakes. *Eeeeek!* He stopped just at the edge of the puddle.

"If you roll into that," said Ginni, "your wheels will slip and slide, and you'll spin round and round, and the diya will fly out!"

Chhotu looked at the puddle. It was not very big. It would be quicker to go straight through. But Ginni was right.

"Then I'll go *around*," said Chhotu. "Slow is better than broken."

So he went the long way, past the big steel pot, past the basket of onions, past Nani's slippers, in a careful curve around the shiny oil. It took a little longer. But the blue diya sat safe and still in the middle carriage.

*Ting-ting!* "Safe and sound!"

Chhotu was nearly at the front door when — *BOOM!*

Outside, someone in the street had burst a big cracker. The window rattled. The pots jingled. Chhotu got such a fright that he rolled backwards and hid behind Nani's slippers, shaking.

"I can't," he whispered. "It's too loud. It's too scary."

From the cage by the window, a green voice spoke. It was **Mithu**, the family parrot, with her red beak and bright eyes.

"I know, I know," said Mithu kindly. "The booms frighten me too. Every Diwali, I put my head under my wing."

"What should I do?" asked Chhotu.

"Take a big breath," said Mithu. "In through your chimney... and out. The booms are loud, but they cannot hurt you in here. And look —" she pointed with her wing — "the door is only ten wheels away."

Chhotu breathed in. *Hhhhh.* He breathed out. *Phhhh.* His wheels stopped shaking.

"Ten wheels," he said. "I can do ten wheels."

"Of course you can," said Mithu. "Brave doesn't mean not scared. Brave means going on, a little bit scared."

Chhotu rolled the last ten wheels to the front door. Through it he could see the courtyard, and the rangoli lotus, and the row of ten little diyas on the doorstep.

And above the rooftops, the sky was deep blue now — and there, just peeping out, was the **first star**.

"Light the diyas!" called Papa.

Arjun came running with a matchbox, which Papa took from him with a smile — matches are for grown-ups. Mummy came, wiping coloured powder off her hands. And Nani came slowly from the kitchen, still looking a tiny bit sad.

"Let's begin," said Nani. "Even without my blue diya."

Just then, she heard a sound by her feet.

*Ting-ting!*

Nani looked down. There was Arjun's little red train. And in its middle carriage, round and blue with white dots like stars...

"My diya!" cried Nani. "My mother's diya! But how...?"

Arjun's eyes went very wide. "Chhotu brought it!" he whispered.

Nani lifted the blue diya out of the carriage as gently as if it were a baby bird. She held it close for a moment. Then she filled it with oil, put in a cotton wick, and Papa struck a match.

The little flame flickered, and grew, and glowed — warm and golden inside the blue clay.

Then Papa helped Arjun light the next diya, and the next, and the next. One, two, three... all ten! Papa switched on the twinkling lights. All along the street, in every house, little lights came on, until the whole of Lucknow was sparkling like the sky.

"Happy Diwali!" everyone said, and hugged.

Nani bent down and picked up Chhotu Chhuk-Chhuk. "Thank you, little train," she whispered. "I don't know how you did it, but thank you."

Chhotu couldn't speak to grown-ups, of course. Toys never do. But his little bell gave the tiniest *ting*.

And in the bedroom, Bhalu smiled his stitched smile. On the shelf, Rani patted her golden ribbon. By the window, Mithu took her head out from under her wing. And behind the kitchen cupboard, Ginni found a whole mathri waiting for her. Nani also wiped up the oil puddle, so nobody would slip.

Later, much later, when the sparklers were finished and the sweets were eaten, Arjun lay in bed. His tummy was full of laddoos. His eyes were full of lights.

On his pillow, right beside him, was Chhotu Chhuk-Chhuk. Arjun wasn't going to put him back in the toy box tonight. Tonight, Chhotu was a hero.

Through the window, Arjun could see the doorstep. The diyas were still burning, small and steady, and the blue one glowed brightest of all.

"Chhotu," Arjun whispered. "Did you really go all the way through the house by yourself?"

Chhotu stayed very still, as toys do when children are watching.

But if Arjun had listened very carefully, he might have heard a tiny voice say:

*"Not by myself. With my friends. One wheel at a time."*

Arjun yawned. His eyes closed. Outside, the last firecracker went *pop* far away, and then everything was quiet and golden and warm.

*Chhuk... chhuk... chhuk...*

*Goodnight, Chhotu. Goodnight, Arjun. Happy Diwali, little one.*

summary: It is Diwali in a house in Lucknow; Nani's special blue diya is lost.
Chhotu, a toy train, finds it in the toy box.
Bhalu the teddy opens the lid and loads the diya.
Rani the rag doll pulls Chhotu over the fluffy rug with her ribbon.
Ginni the mouse shows a ramp down the kitchen step.
Chhotu goes around a slippery oil puddle: slow is better than broken.
Mithu the parrot helps him breathe and be brave when crackers boom.
Chhotu delivers the diya just as the first star appears.
Diwali means a row of lamps: light over darkness, kindness and sharing.
Big jobs are done one small step at a time, with friends.

rd-stories-clocktower-shimla.title: The Clock That Stopped at 4:17
rd-stories-clocktower-shimla.subtitle: A hill-school mystery: a stopped clock, a missing trophy and a message hidden in plain sight.

sections.md:
Every good mystery is a fair game between the writer and the reader. All the clues you need to solve this one are placed in the story *before* the answer is revealed. Read slowly. Notice times, weather, and who says what.

Our detective is **Meher Sood**, fourteen, a boarder at a hill school above Shimla who keeps a notebook of 'things that don't fit'. Her partner, whether he likes it or not, is **Kabir Thapa**, who knows every pipe, wire and shortcut on campus because his father is the school's electrician.

> Tip: keep a list of suspects as you read and cross names off only when you have a reason.

sections.h: After reading: how Meher solved it
sections.md:
Meher's method is one you can use in science and in life:

1. **Write down facts, not feelings.** 'Dev looks guilty' is a feeling. 'Dev's shoes were wet' is a fact.
2. **Line up the times.** A timeline shows who *could* have been where.
3. **Ask what is missing.** The trophy is missing — but so is the sound the clock should have made.
4. **Test the explanation.** Kabir's ladder test proved the clock could be stopped from inside.

The twist hides in the most ordinary clue: the clock itself. People trusted it, so nobody questioned it.

sections.md:
- **Trust and evidence.** We often believe something because it has always been reliable — a clock, a teacher, a rumour.
- **Pressure to win.** The theft grew out of fear of disappointing others, not greed.
- **Owning mistakes.** The ending is not about punishment but about repair.

*Did you know?* Many real Indian hill stations, like Shimla, have colonial-era clock towers that were once the only public timekeepers for whole towns.

check.q: Which best describes the culprit's motive?
options: Fear of failing others and shame
check.why: The story shows the culprit acted out of pressure and shame about losing, which is why the ending focuses on making things right.

parts.md:
The hailstorm came over the ridge at five minutes to four, and by the time the umpire's whistle had stopped echoing, the cricket field of St. Aldric's School looked like someone had spilled a sack of white marbles across it.

Meher Sood ran with everyone else to the shelter of the old stone corridor. She was not thinking about cricket. She was thinking about the inter-house trophy — a silver cup with two curling handles, older than the school's oldest teacher — because it was supposed to be presented at assembly the next morning, and Mr. Rawat had carried it up to the trophy room only an hour ago, polished so bright you could read the time in it.

She was thinking about it because she had seen something odd. As she ran past the clock tower, the great iron hands had been shivering, as if the clock were cold.

She wrote it in her notebook while the hail drummed on the tin roof: *3:58 — tower clock hands shaking. Wind? Not that windy.*

Kabir Thapa leaned over her shoulder, dripping. “You are writing in a hailstorm.”

“Things that don't fit,” she said, “don't wait for good weather.”

He snorted, but he looked up at the tower too. Kabir had grown up in the staff quarters behind the kitchen. His father kept the school's lights burning and its old boiler grumbling. If anybody knew whether a clock was supposed to shiver, it was Kabir.

“Gears,” he said finally. “Somebody's in the gear room.”

“Nobody's allowed in the gear room.”

“Exactly,” said Kabir.

The trophy was gone by dinner.

The news travelled through the dining hall faster than the dal. Mr. Rawat had locked the trophy room at four o'clock sharp — he said so loudly, to anyone who would listen, his moustache trembling. When he went back at five with the house captains to rehearse the presentation, the lock was still closed, the window was still latched, and the velvet stand in the glass case was empty.

“A locked room,” whispered Ananya Bhatt, the head girl, to the table. She sounded almost delighted. Then she remembered her duties and added, “This is very serious.”

The principal, Mrs. Kaul, stood up and tapped her glass. She did not shout. She never shouted, which was far more frightening. “The cup will be returned to my office by tomorrow morning,” she said. “No questions will be asked. If it is not, every house will lose its points for the term.”

A groan rolled across the hall like distant thunder. Dev Malhotra, captain of Himalaya House, put his head in his hands. Himalaya had been losing the match badly when the hail arrived. Everyone knew it. Some people, Meher noticed, were already looking at Dev.

She opened her notebook under the table. *Locked door. Locked window. Trophy room is on the second floor of the tower building — directly below the clock.*

She underlined the last word twice.

After lights-out, Meher did something she had never done before: she broke a rule on purpose.

She met Kabir at the back stairs of the tower building. He had a torch, a screwdriver and the expression of someone who already regretted this.

“If my father finds out—”

“Then we tell him we found the trophy,” said Meher. “Fathers forgive a lot when you find trophies.”

The stairs smelled of damp stone and old varnish. On the second floor, the trophy room door was exactly as Mr. Rawat had described: heavy teak, a brass padlock, no scratches. Kabir shone the torch on the floor. The dust on the landing had been swept — recently, in neat curves.

“Who sweeps a landing nobody uses?” Meher murmured.

They climbed to the third floor, to the narrow iron door of the gear room. It was not locked. Inside, the clock's heart filled the space: wheels as big as bicycle tyres, a long pendulum hanging still, and above them, through slats, the back of the clock face. Kabir whistled softly.

“It's stopped,” he said. “Pendulum's dead still. Somebody pushed this—” he pointed to a thin steel rod wedged between two teeth of the biggest wheel “—into the gears. That's why the hands were shaking. The motor kept trying to turn them.”

Meher looked through the slats. Seen from behind, the hands read backwards, but she worked it out: **4:17**.

“So the clock stopped at 4:17,” she said slowly. “And everyone who looked at it this afternoon thought it was 4:17 for a very long time.”

In the morning, Meher interviewed the suspects. She did not call them suspects to their faces. She called them 'people who might have noticed something', which was polite and also true.

Ananya Bhatt said she had been in the library from four till half past four. “I checked the tower clock when I came out,” she said. “It said 4:17, which was strange, because I was sure I'd been there longer. I thought my watch was fast.”

Ms. D'Souza, the music teacher, said she had been practising the chapel organ from four o'clock. “I play the same hymn three times, always. It takes about twelve minutes. I finished, looked out of the window at the tower, and it said 4:17. So I thought — good, five minutes to spare, I'll play it once more.”

Meher wrote that down very carefully.

Dev Malhotra would barely speak. “I never went near the tower,” he said, staring at the floor. His school shoes, Meher noticed, had a pale grey crust around the soles. Not mud. Something finer.

Bahadur ji, the night watchman, was sitting in the sun outside the kitchen with a glass of tea. “The bell,” he said, before she could even ask. “That clock rings once on the half hour. Yesterday it rang once at — I don't know — maybe twenty to five? I thought, the old thing has gone mad. Then it was quiet.”

*A bell at 4:40,* Meher wrote. *But the clock was jammed at 4:17. A jammed clock can't ring.*

Unless someone unjammed it for a moment.

“Grey crust,” said Kabir, at lunch, rubbing a pinch of powder between his fingers. Meher had scraped it, apologising, from the edge of the landing outside the trophy room. “It's not dirt. It's graphite.”

“Pencil lead?”

“Lock lubricant. My father uses it on old padlocks so they don't stick. You puff it into the keyhole.” He looked at her. “Someone opened that padlock with a key and then oiled it so it wouldn't squeak.”

“So it isn't a locked-room mystery at all,” said Meher. “It's a person-with-a-key mystery.”

“Who has keys?”

She counted on her fingers. “Mr. Rawat. The principal's office. The bursar. And” — she stopped — “the house captains, during sports week, to set up the presentation.”

Kabir winced. “Dev.”

“Dev had graphite on his shoes,” Meher said. “But think. If Dev took it, why jam the clock? He'd just take it and walk away. The clock is the strange part. Somebody wanted people to believe something happened at 4:17.”

Kabir chewed slowly. “Or wanted people to believe they were somewhere at 4:17.”

Meher sat very still. Then she turned back three pages in her notebook and read Ms. D'Souza's words again: *I play it three times. It takes about twelve minutes.*

That afternoon they did an experiment. Kabir called it 'science'. Meher called it 'checking'.

Kabir's father had to oil the clock once a year, so there was a proper ladder and a logbook in the gear room. Kabir pulled the steel rod free. Slowly, groaning, the great wheel turned, the pendulum began to swing, and outside, the hands crept forward. Meher stood in the courtyard with a stopwatch.

“If someone pulls the rod out,” Kabir shouted down, “the clock catches up a little and the half-hour striker can trip once. Then if they push it back—” He pushed it. The hands froze. *Clang,* went the bell, once, startled.

“That's the bell Bahadur ji heard!” Meher shouted back. “Someone came up here again at about 4:40, pulled the rod, then jammed it again.”

“Why?”

“To get the rod back for a moment? To check the time?” She frowned. “No. To make sure the hands still said 4:17 after the clock jumped. They had to reset it.”

On the logbook's last page, under Kabir's father's neat entries, there was a smudge of grey graphite and a single long hair, dark, tied with a thin blue ribbon the colour of the school's prefect badges.

Meher did not touch it. She photographed it with Kabir's cracked phone instead.

Meher laid it all out on the library table that evening, using salt cellars borrowed from the dining hall as people.

“Fact one,” she said. “The hail started at 3:55. Everyone ran inside. Nobody was outside watching the tower.

“Fact two: Mr. Rawat locked up at four. Fact three: someone opened the padlock with a key and used graphite so it wouldn't squeak. Fact four: the clock was jammed at 4:17.

“Now, Ms. D'Souza. She started playing at four. She plays twelve minutes, so she finished at about 4:12. She looked at the tower and saw 4:17. That means by 4:12, *real time*, the clock already said 4:17. It was jammed *before* 4:17. Somebody set the hands a few minutes ahead and stopped them.”

Kabir frowned. “Why ahead?”

“Because of Ananya,” said Meher quietly. “Ananya said she left the library and the clock said 4:17. If she really left at 4:30, the clock gives her an alibi — but a wrong one. She thinks she was in the library until 4:17, and everyone thinks the theft happened later, while she was walking back with witnesses.”

“So Ananya's innocent?”

“Ananya,” Meher said, “never said she was in the library alone.”

Meher found the librarian's sign-in register. Ananya's neat signature was there: *IN 3:58*. And just below it, in a hurried hand: *Priya Negi, IN 3:59*. There was no *OUT* time for Priya at all.

Priya Negi was vice-captain of Himalaya House. She wore her long dark hair tied in a blue prefect's ribbon. She was the best student in the school at physics and had once won a prize for repairing the chemistry lab's broken balance.

She was also, Meher remembered, the one who had to make the speech at assembly whenever Himalaya lost — and Himalaya had lost the trophy for six years running.

Meher did not go to Mrs. Kaul. Not yet. She went to the music room where Priya sat alone at the piano, not playing.

“The clock was clever,” Meher said gently. “You set it to 4:17 so people would remember the wrong time. You came back at 4:40 to fix the hands after they slipped. And you used graphite from the house captains' kit because Dev had the key and you borrowed it from his blazer. That's why his shoes were grey — he walked through the landing after you, looking for his key.”

Priya's hands lay on the keys. For a long moment there was no sound in the room at all.

“I wasn't going to keep it,” Priya said at last. Her voice was very small. “I just — every year I stand up and say *well played, everyone*, and they clap for the other house, and my father asks on the phone whether we won, and I say *next year*. I thought if there was no trophy, there would be no ceremony. Just one year without the speech.”

She pointed upward. “It's in the gear room. Inside the clock case, behind the pendulum. Nobody looks there.”

Meher sat down next to her on the piano bench. “Dev nearly got blamed,” she said.

“I know.” Priya wiped her face with her sleeve. “I was going to tell. I kept thinking: *at assembly, I'll tell*. Then *after assembly*.” She almost laughed. “I kept stopping the clock.”

They went to Mrs. Kaul's office together, the three of them — Meher, Priya and, a little behind, Kabir carrying the silver cup wrapped in his father's dust-cloth.

Mrs. Kaul listened to the whole thing without interrupting. Then she said, “Thank you for bringing it back.” And to Priya: “We will talk about consequences. We will also talk about why a trophy felt heavier than the truth.”

At assembly the next morning, the cup shone on its velvet stand. The tower clock, oiled and set right by Kabir's father, struck nine exactly on time. And when Himalaya House lost the trophy for the seventh year running, it was Dev who stood up and said *well played*, while Priya, beside him, clapped the loudest of anyone.

In her notebook, Meher wrote the last line of the case: *The clock was never lying. We just stopped asking it questions.*

summary: A trophy vanishes from a locked room below a school clock tower during a hailstorm.
The tower clock was deliberately jammed so witnesses would remember a false time of 4:17.
Graphite lock lubricant showed the padlock was opened with a key, not forced.
Ms. D'Souza's twelve-minute organ practice proved the clock already read 4:17 by about 4:12.
A single 'wrong' bell at 4:40 revealed someone returned to reset the hands.
The library register showed Priya Negi signed in but never out.
Priya borrowed Dev's key; Dev's grey shoes came from searching for it later.
Motive was pressure and shame, not greed.
Meher's method: facts over feelings, timelines, ask what is missing, test explanations.
The ending focuses on honesty and repair rather than punishment.

rd-stories-gappu-trumpet.title: Gappu and the Lost Trumpet
rd-stories-gappu-trumpet.subtitle: A baby elephant in Kerala who can only squeak learns that every voice has its moment.

sections.md:
Tonight we are going to the green, rainy forests of **Kerala**, where coconut palms sway and the rivers are wide and slow.

There lives a baby elephant called **Gappu**. All the grown-up elephants have big, booming trumpets: *PAAWOOO!* But when Gappu lifts his trunk, all that comes out is a tiny *squeak!*

Grown-ups: you can make the sounds! Big trumpet for Amma, tiny squeak for Gappu, a *mee-ow* for the peacock and a *kuhoo* for the koel. Children love joining in.

sections.md:
Gappu is make-believe, but his family is a lot like real **Asian elephants**, which live in the forests of Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Assam and other parts of India.

- 👵 **Grandmother leads.** An elephant herd is a family of mothers, aunties, sisters and babies, led by the oldest, wisest female — just like Muthassi. She remembers where water and food can be found.
- 🍼 **Babies stay close.** A baby elephant (a *calf*) drinks its mother's milk for a long time and walks right beside her. Aunties help look after the little ones.
- 👃 **The trunk is a nose and a hand.** An elephant's trunk can smell, breathe, drink, lift a log, pick a single blade of grass, give a hug — and make sounds.
- 🔊 **Many sounds.** Elephants trumpet when excited or alarmed, rumble to keep in touch, and baby elephants really do squeak and squeal!
- 🌳 **Gardeners of the forest.** Elephants open paths and spread seeds in their dung, helping new trees to grow.

India has more wild Asian elephants than any other country. They are protected by law, and in many places forest guards and villagers work together to keep both elephants and people safe.

check.q: Who usually leads a real elephant herd?
check.why: An elephant herd is led by its oldest female, called the matriarch, who remembers where water and food are.

sections.h: Loud and soft: a listening game
sections.md:
Gappu learnt that loud is not always better. Try this game at home:

1. **Loud or soft?** A grown-up names a sound. Children stretch their arms wide for LOUD and make themselves tiny for soft. *A train horn* (loud!), *a cat purring* (soft), *a temple bell* (loud), *falling leaves* (soft), *Amma's trumpet* (LOUD), *Gappu's squeak* (tiny).
2. **Whisper telephone.** Sit in a circle and whisper a message, like *'Gappu found Kunju in the log'*, from ear to ear. Soft voices need careful listening!
3. **When do we use a soft voice?** When a baby is sleeping, in a library, when someone is sad or frightened, at night.
4. **When do we use a big voice?** When calling for help, when cheering at a cricket match, when singing in a group.

> Did you know? Doctors and teachers often speak softly to children who are scared — just like Gappu did — because gentle voices help us feel safe.

parts.md:
Far away in Kerala, where the rain falls warm and the rivers wind like green ribbons, there lived a herd of elephants.

There was Muthassi, the grandmother elephant, who was very old and very wise. There was Amma, who was big and gentle and grey as a rain cloud. There were aunties and cousins, all splashing and munching and swinging their trunks.

And there was **Gappu**.

Gappu was the smallest elephant in the herd. He had floppy pink-edged ears, a wiggly little trunk, and a tail with a tuft at the end like a paintbrush.

Every morning the herd walked down to the river. And every morning, when they got there, Amma lifted her great trunk to the sky and called out:

**"PAAAWOOOO!"**

The sound rolled over the water. It bounced off the hills. Birds flew up from the trees. It meant: *Good morning, forest! The elephants are here!*

Then all the aunties trumpeted. **PAWOO! PAWOO!** And all the cousins trumpeted. **Pawoo! Pawoo!**

And then Gappu lifted his little trunk, took a deep breath, puffed out his cheeks and...

*squeak.*

That was all. One tiny squeak, like a door that needs oil.

The cousins giggled. Gappu's ears drooped.

"Amma," said Gappu that evening, as they stood under a big jackfruit tree. "Why can't I trumpet like you?"

Amma stroked his head with the tip of her trunk. "You are still little, my Gappu. Your voice will grow when you grow."

"But I want it *now*," said Gappu. "Everyone laughs at my squeak."

That night Gappu could not sleep. He lay curled against Amma's warm side and listened to the frogs singing *krok-krok* and the rain pattering on the leaves.

"Maybe my trumpet is lost," he thought. "Maybe I had a big trumpet once, and I dropped it somewhere. If I find it, I'll be loud like everyone else!"

So, very early next morning, when the sky was still pale pink, Gappu tiptoed away from the sleeping herd. (Elephants can tiptoe, you know. They have soft, cushiony feet.)

"I'm going to find my lost trumpet," he whispered. "I'll be back before breakfast."

*Do you think a trumpet can really get lost?*

The first animal Gappu met was **Mayil**, the peacock, standing in a clearing with his tail spread wide like a shimmering green-and-blue fan.

"MEE-OWW! MEE-OWW!" called Mayil, so loudly that a squirrel dropped its nut.

"Excuse me," said Gappu. "That's a very big voice. Did you find it somewhere? I've lost mine."

Mayil laughed and shook his feathers. "Find it? Little one, this voice grew with me. I call loudly when I feel the rain coming. Try it, if you like!"

Gappu lifted his trunk. "Mee... ow?" he tried. It came out as *mee-squeak*. Mayil was kind and did not laugh.

Next, from a mango tree, came a sweet, high song: *kuhoo... kuhoo...* It was **Kuyil**, the koel bird, black and shiny with red eyes.

"What a beautiful song," sighed Gappu. "Could I borrow it?"

"A song can't be borrowed," sang Kuyil gently. "Each of us has our own. Mine is for the mango season. Yours is for... well, you'll find out."

Gappu walked on, puzzled. Everyone's voice seemed to be just right for *them*. But what was a squeak just right for?

Gappu walked along the riverbank. He looked under a rock. No trumpet. He looked inside a big lotus leaf. Only a frog, who said *krok* rather crossly.

High above him, in a coconut palm, sat a small brown bird with a bright yellow eye. It was **Kuruvi**, the myna.

"What are you looking for, little one?" chirped Kuruvi.

"My trumpet," said Gappu. "My big loud voice. I think I lost it."

Kuruvi tilted her head. "Hmm. I can fly up high and look all around. Wait here."

She zoomed up, up, above the palm trees, circled once, twice, and came swooping back down.

"I didn't see any trumpets," she said. "But I did see something else. Over by the old banyan tree, Kunju's mother is crying. Her baby monkey is lost!"

"Lost?" said Gappu. "Like my trumpet?"

"Much more important than a trumpet," said Kuruvi. "Come on!"

Under the huge old banyan tree, with its roots hanging down like curtains, sat **Kunju's mother**. She was a grey langur monkey with a black face, and big tears were rolling down her cheeks.

"My Kunju went to play," she sobbed, "and now he won't come back. I've called and called!"

Just then the whole elephant herd came stomping through the trees. They had woken up and found Gappu missing!

"Gappu!" cried Amma. "You frightened me!" She wrapped her trunk around him in a big hug. Then she saw the crying monkey. "What's wrong?"

When she heard, Amma said, "Don't worry. I'll call him." She lifted her trunk and —

**"PAAAWOOOO!"**

The sound was so loud that the leaves shook. Somewhere nearby, there was a tiny frightened squeal, and then — silence.

"Oh no," said Kunju's mother. "He's scared! When he's scared, he hides and won't come out."

The aunties tried calling. **PAWOO!** The silence got even quieter. Mayil the peacock tried. **MEE-OWW!** Nothing. The cousins tried. **Pawoo!** Nothing.

Big loud voices were making Kunju *more* frightened, not less.

Then a slow, wrinkly voice spoke from beside the stream.

"Shouting won't help."

It was **Ammu**, the old tortoise. She was so old that her shell had moss on it.

"I've lived in this forest a hundred years," said Ammu. "When little ones are frightened, they hide in small places. There's an old hollow log just past the bamboo. I'd look there."

They all hurried — well, the elephants hurried; Ammu came along slowly — to the bamboo grove. There, lying on its side, was a long, hollow log, covered in ferns. It had a hole at one end, a very small hole.

From deep inside came a tiny sniffle.

"Kunju?" called his mother softly. But the log was long and twisty, and her voice didn't go far enough in.

Amma tried to put her trunk inside. It was much too big. It wouldn't even fit in the hole.

"If I trumpet," said Amma, "I'll scare him even more."

Everyone was quiet. And then Muthassi, the grandmother elephant, turned her wise old eyes and looked at... **Gappu**.

"Gappu," she said. "Your trunk is small. And your voice is gentle. Will you try?"

Gappu's heart went *thump-thump-thump*.

He walked up to the log. He looked at the tiny hole. Then, very carefully, he slid the tip of his little trunk inside. It fitted!

He took a small breath. Not a big, puffed-up breath. Just a soft one. And he made the gentlest sound he knew:

*squeak... squeak...*

It sounded friendly. It sounded like someone small, just like Kunju. It didn't sound scary at all.

Inside the log, the sniffling stopped.

*squeak?* went Gappu again, as if to say, *Hello? It's only me.*

And from deep inside came a tiny reply: "...hello?"

"Hello, Kunju," whispered Gappu through his trunk. "I'm Gappu. Your Amma is here. Nobody is going to shout any more. Do you want to hold my trunk?"

There was a little scrabble, and then Gappu felt two tiny hands holding the tip of his trunk.

Very, very slowly, Gappu stepped backwards. And out of the log, blinking in the light, came **Kunju**, the baby monkey, holding on tight.

"KUNJU!" cried his mother, and scooped him up in her arms. She hugged him and kissed his little black face over and over.

The elephants cheered — quietly, so as not to frighten anyone again. They swung their trunks and stamped their feet softly. Kuruvi the myna sang a happy song from the bamboo. Kuyil joined in with a *kuhoo*. Even old Ammu the tortoise smiled a slow, wrinkly smile.

Kunju's mother turned to Gappu. "Thank you," she said. "Only *you* could have done that. A big voice would never have reached my baby."

Gappu's ears went pink right to the edges.

Amma wrapped her trunk around him. "You see, Gappu? You didn't lose anything. Your voice was right here all along — and today it was exactly the voice we needed."

"But one day," asked Gappu, "will I trumpet like you?"

"One day," said Amma, "you'll be big, and you'll trumpet across the whole valley. But I hope you'll always remember how to squeak, too."

*What did Gappu learn about his small voice?*

On the way back to the river, Kunju would not let go of Gappu. He rode on Gappu's little back, holding his floppy ears like the handles of a bicycle.

"Why did you hide in the log?" Gappu asked him.

"I was chasing a butterfly," said Kunju, "and then I couldn't see my Amma. And then a big, BIG noise came, and I got so scared that I crawled in and couldn't remember how to come out."

"I get scared too," said Gappu. "This morning I ran away to find my trumpet. That was silly. I should have told Amma."

"Next time," said Kunju wisely, "we both tell our Ammas."

"Promise," said Gappu.

At the riverbank, Kunju's mother gave Gappu a bunch of ripe yellow bananas as a thank-you present. Gappu shared them with all his cousins — even the ones who had giggled. They didn't giggle any more. One cousin, Chinnu, said shyly, "Gappu, can you teach me to squeak like that?"

And for the rest of the afternoon, the riverbank was full of the funniest sound: big elephants trying to make tiny squeaks, and laughing until they fell in the water. *SPLASH!*

That evening, the herd walked back to the river. The sky turned orange, then purple, then deep blue. The first stars came out over the coconut palms.

Amma lifted her trunk: **"PAAAWOOOO!"** *Goodnight, forest!*

The aunties trumpeted. The cousins trumpeted.

Then everyone turned and looked at Gappu. Nobody giggled this time. They waited.

Gappu lifted his little trunk, took a small, happy breath, and said:

*squeak!*

And from the banyan tree, far away, a tiny monkey voice called back: *"Goodnight, Gappu!"*

Gappu curled up against Amma's warm, rain-cloud side. The frogs sang *krok-krok*. The rain began to patter softly on the leaves. Somewhere, Kuruvi tucked her head under her wing, and Mayil folded up his great fan of a tail.

Gappu yawned a big elephant yawn. His eyes grew heavy.

"Amma," he mumbled, "I think my trumpet was never lost."

"No, my Gappu," said Amma softly. "It was just waiting for the right day."

And Gappu fell fast asleep, dreaming of rivers and stars and the sound of a tiny squeak that saved the day.

*Goodnight, Gappu. Goodnight, little one.*

rd-stories-itarsi-junction.title: Itarsi Junction, 3 a.m.
rd-stories-itarsi-junction.subtitle: A missed connection, a tea-stall, and one long night in the middle of India.

sections.md:
Itarsi in Madhya Pradesh is one of the great crossroads of Indian Railways — lines from Delhi, Mumbai, Howrah and the south meet there, and trains pass through at every hour. This story takes place on its platforms over a single night.

**Kunal**, nineteen, is on his way from Delhi to Pune to sit an entrance exam his father has chosen for him. He misses his connection. **Shakuntala-bai**, sixty-something, runs a tea-stall on Platform 4 and has watched a million travellers come and go. Between midnight and dawn, very little happens — and everything changes.

The story is told in the present tense, hour by hour.
